4.6 Alpha—A ‘Business First’ Approach
In line with observations drawn from the application of the DDBM3, a ‘business
first’ approach was identified at Alpha. Here, it was mainly the business side, i.e.,
customers, who initiated the transformation actions, as they demanded data delivery.
These actions were followed by some measures that developed the maturity of the
upper levels of the EA (e.g., strategic initiatives and new roles). However, weak-
nesses remained in the lower EA—e.g., in the data analysis capability or the scaling
of networked machines.
Insights On Action Taken for DDBM Transformation “[...] actually, our [busi-
ness] customers triggered us to provide data-driven services. They clearly demanded
access to machinery data.This triggered the process of thinking aboutall relevant re-
quirements to realize this business opportunityandto create more services [...]” (A1).
Starting from the ‘business model’ area, Alpha’s DDBM transformation began with
increasing customer demand for access to machine data. The service department ini-
tiated the provision of data that had, until that point, only been used internally. Next,
Alpha’s management established a customer-oriented strategic initiative to explore
DDBM, starting with a clear business perspective and employing associated tools
and methods (e.g., business model canvas, value proposition design, etc.). Alpha
then launched new external applications (e.g., digital service portals, end-user apps)
which were developed to create digital channels for data-driven service provision.
Alpha subsequently defined new ‘processes’ for developing and operating data-
driven services and associated roles on the ‘people and applications’ layer. These
included digital product managers as bridgeheads between technology development
and business management (A2). However, the acquisition of data analytics compe-
tencies to match these roles and the provision of appropriate tooling remain a key
challenge for Alpha, resulting in lower maturity of these capability areas. On the

readiness_statement: Organizations with a single, non-diversified line of business tend to structure EA functions around traditional EA domains (business, application, data, infrastructure architects serving the whole enterprise), while organizations with diversified business activities structure EA functions around business areas/lines of business instead, with domain architects reserved mainly for purely technical domains (integration, infrastructure, security); more precisely, which EA domains are centralized versus decentralized tracks the organization's operating model (per Ross et al. 2006: diversification/coordination/replication/unification) -- domains tied to processes/applications decentralize under low process standardization, while domains tied to shared data centralize under high data integration.
mechanism: Process standardization and data integration requirements (the two dimensions of operating model) determine which EA domains benefit from being planned globally (by domain architects) versus locally (by business-area architects); imposing one fixed structure regardless of these requirements creates mismatches between architecture team design and actual coordination needs.
operationalization_hint: Diagnose an organization's operating model (standardization and integration levels) before designing/evaluating its EA function structure, and expect domain-based, business-area-based, and hybrid structures to each be correct for different operating-model profiles rather than treating any one as universally "best practice."
rationale: The paper links business diversification to business-area alignment and explains how process standardization and data integration determine decentralised, domain-based and hybrid arrangements. The CF accurately represents this contingent-structure argument.

5.3.4 Alignment with Operating Models
The structure of EA functions in organizations aligns with
their operating models. An operating model in this context
is understood specifically in the way defined by Ross et al.
(2006, p. 25) as ‘‘the necessary level of business process
integration and standardization for delivering goods and
services to customers’’. Ross et al. (2006) distinguish four
different operating models: diversification (implies low
process standardization and integration across different
business units), coordination (implies low process stan-
dardization, but high process integration), replication (im-
plies high process standardization, but low process
integration) and unification (implies high process stan-
dardization and integration across different business units).
These two dimensions of operating models – standardiza-
tion and integration – essentially define the structure of EA
functions in terms of necessary architecture positions.
Namely, business process standardization across differ-
ent business units clearly relates to the presence of spe-
cialized architects focusing on different business areas, as
suggested by Proposition 3.1 described earlier. On the one
hand, organizations operating according to the models that
imply low process standardization (i.e. diversification and
coordination) require dedicated architects to serve their
individual business units (often independent lines of busi-
ness and interrelated business functions respectively). On
the other hand, companies implementing the operating
models with high process standardization (i.e. replication
and unification) may not need such architects and instead
employ only ‘‘general’’ business and application architects
embracing all their business activities. Similarly, organi-
zations with operating models that imply high data inte-
gration (i.e. coordination and unification) are likely to
benefit from employing specialized data architects to define
common information models and exchange formats for all
their business units.

organizations with more ‘‘consolidated’’ (i.e. more highly
standardized and integrated) operating models may need
more domain architects to focus on EA domains whose
‘‘contents’’ are common to all their business units, as
suggested by Proposition 3.2 described earlier. Put it sim-
ply, an operating model with its standardization and inte-
gration requirements defines which EA domains should be
planned globally by the respective domain architects and
which EA domains should be planned locally in business
units by architects knowledgeable in the specific activities
of these units. This conclusion can be summarized into the
following theoretical proposition:
Proposition 3.4: Architecture positions in EA functions
are aligned with the process standardization and integra-
tion requirements of the adopted operating models.

mechanism: Because the properties that actually determine EA function structure (IT size, diversification, operating model) vary independently of industry classification, treating "industry" as a design factor for EA function structure (as many industry benchmarks implicitly do) conflates a non-causal correlate with the actual causal drivers.

5.3.6 Industry Influence on Structure
The available evidence suggests that the industry in which
organizations operate actually does not influence the
structure of their EA functions in any particular fashion.
Among all organizations analyzed in this study represent-
ing very diverse industry sectors (see Table 1), no articu-
late industry-specific patterns of structuring EA functions
were identified. Although the impact of industry was
noticeable in some other aspects of their EA practices (e.g.
planning horizon and stakeholder rotation), the structure of
their EA functions proved to be industry-neutral. This
conclusion can be summarized into the following last
theoretical proposition:
Proposition 3.6: The structure of the EA function does
not depend directly on the industry of the organization.

Also, as per Proposition 3.6, the structure of EA func-
tions does not depend on the industry of organizations.
Together with the previous observation of Kotusev (2019)
that the sets of utilized EA artifacts are also industry-in-
dependent, this proposition furthers the view that the
general mechanisms of EA practices are universal and
industry-neutral.

rationale: The case states that harmonised DDA requires an incremental approach with interim consensus states and that phased change mitigates resistance and supports commitment. The CF accurately frames interim architectures as a staged transformation practice.

Phase I necessitates significant organizational, functional, and cultural transformations
in how the Global R&D data are organized and governed. It involves defining which teams
are accountable for data, clarifying their roles and responsibilities and establishing the
role of data and their value within the organization. However, it can be challenging to
immediately discern the tangible benefits associated with each element of the foundational
phase, as their value may be realized over time, during the subsequent execution phase.
Consequently, a comprehensive change management effort was required to socialize the
framework. This effort involved conducting pre-assessments and presenting the draft
framework to stakeholders to integrate their feedback and refine the roadmap. This
approach contributed to a smooth and steady acceptance of the change and fostered
stakeholder commitment.

Despite being named Data Fabric, Phase I of the strategy incorporates most elements
from the Data Mesh concept, showing that Data Mesh and Data Fabric can complement
each other effectively. Whilst Data Mesh lays the organizational and mindset foundation for
how enterprise data are organized and managed, Data Fabric establishes the technological
basis for the data architecture. By carefully blending the most suitable components of these
two concepts and customizing them to fit the specific needs of the enterprise, we developed
a comprehensive roadmap for implementation and evolution.
The ongoing debate between proponents of Data Mesh and Data Fabric often revolves
around the perceived superiority of one approach over the other. However, our case study
has demonstrated the effectiveness of a complementary approach. This approach has
garnered high acceptance and commitment from stakeholders and leadership, validating
its efficacy thus far.
By embracing the strengths of both paradigms, the Pharma company has fostered an
environment where organizational and technical aspects converge harmoniously. The FLM
adopted during Phase I enabled data leaders of distributed and autonomous DDs to steer
the data vision and roadmaps, facilitating the seamless orchestration of key stakeholders
and efficient execution of objectives.

the Data strategy is crucial for the Pharma company. A corporate strategy aims to establish
a common “framework language” to ensure interoperability, while providing the necessary
agility and flexibility to adapt to division-specific needs.
Deviation from this balance towards centralization could lead to non-acceptance
and a lack of commitment, particularly if the unique needs and intricacies of individual
divisions are not adequately considered. It might also entail an unreasonable amount
of alignment effort to develop a global approach that can effectively accommodate the
diverse requirements of a large-scale organization. On the other hand, ignoring the need
for a global Data strategy and maintaining decentralized local strategies could result in
“misunderstandings” or a lack of interoperability between the divisions. For example, if
each division has a different definition of DPs and uses different technologies to store,
search, and share DPs, this approach might improve data transparency, discoverability, and
reusability within one division, but could create even more siloed data ecosystems within
the entire organization.
This balance is highly individual for each organization, being dependent on the
corporate culture, organizational structure, industry specifics, maturity of digital and data
capabilities, and many other internal and external determinants. Moreover, this balance
may evolve with the organization’s digital and data maturity. Companies may initially
adopt a highly centralized data strategy and gradually move towards decentralization, or
vice versa. In our case, elements of the data strategy were initially pursued separately in a
decentralized manner across different organizations within the pharmaceutical company.
However, as the need for a global data strategy became apparent at the global management
level, the initiative for a global Data Product strategy was launched.
Notably, as of the time of publishing this paper, a global Data Product strategy was ini-
tiated in the Pharma company that confirms that the expressed necessity was acknowledged

The unique design and implementation decisions made within the Pharma company were
deeply influenced by the organization’s internal and external factors, including corporate
culture, existing architecture, strategic objectives, ongoing initiatives, market conditions,
financial considerations, and more. Therefore, while the case study serves as a guiding
reference, its direct replication without careful adaptation may not yield the same results
in other organizational contexts. For instance, the Global R&D had already fostered a
culture of agility, robust cross-functional collaboration, and a readiness for continuous
improvement and change. This pre-existing disposition facilitated the acceptance and
commitment to transformative frameworks like DDA. Conversely, organizations with
more conservative or less mature enterprise ecosystems in these aspects might face greater
challenges in achieving a similar level of commitment, necessitating the consideration of

The Integrated Strategic Enterprise Architecture (ISEA) framework (Figure 1) adopts a
three-layer structure that integrates strategic planning and enterprise execution. The top
layer, Strategic Architecture (SA), encompasses four strategic dimensions: customer, prod-
ucts, staff, and capacity. The middle layer, Enterprise Architecture (EA), includes TOGAF
standard domains such as business, information, application, and technology. The SA layer
and EA layer are tightly connected through a bidirectional cycle: strategic architecture pro-
vides “strategy guidance” downward to ensure EA development aligns with organizational
strategic objectives, while enterprise architecture feeds back “capability feedback” upward,
conveying practical considerations such as technical feasibility, execution capability, and
resource constraints to the strategy layer. This dynamic synergy mechanism breaks the
traditional unidirectional planning model, forming a continuously optimized closed-loop
system that ultimately integrates at the bottom layer into a complete ISEA framework,
achieving alignment between strategic intent and technical practice. This model is particu-
larly suitable for large-scale multi-purpose sports venues promoting ESGI transformation,
where both clear sustainable development strategic direction and consideration of existing
IT systems, operational capabilities, and resource allocation realities are needed. Through
the ISEA framework, these diverse requirements can be systematically integrated.
Figure 1. The Integrated Strategic Enterprise Architecture (ISEA) framework.
Strategic Architecture (SA), like a brain, provides directional guidance for the entire
enterprise architecture, while EA supports SA. SA defines organizational vision and objec-
tives, guiding enterprise architecture downward, where business architecture transforms
strategic intent into concrete business directions and further guides the development of data
architecture, application architecture, and technology architecture. This relationship ex-
hibits dynamic bidirectional interaction characteristics, with strategic architecture guiding
the development of each architectural layer top-down while obtaining feedback from the

raw_condition_label: operational business-IT alignment requires continuous, multi-technique diagnostic assessment rather than a one-time check
readiness_statement: Because legacy information systems continuously accumulate incremental changes (technical debt, ad hoc adaptations, evolving business processes), operational business-IT alignment cannot be assessed once and assumed stable; it requires periodically repeated diagnostic assessment combining quantitative metrics (implementation/representation link counts and rates), qualitative consistency rules (cross-checking functional and data-dimension links), and anti-pattern detection (e.g., pure technical integration, functional silo, monolithic application, multiple functional implementations) to reveal areas of drift.
mechanism: Single-technique assessment (e.g., metrics alone) can mask or mis-signal misalignment -- e.g., a high rate of "unimplemented" business concepts may simply reflect composite/aggregated business processes rather than a true gap -- so triangulating multiple complementary diagnostic lenses reduces false positives/negatives and gives architects actionable, targeted evolution priorities rather than an undifferentiated alignment score.
operationalization_hint: Assess operational alignment using at least three complementary lenses -- coverage/implementation-rate metrics, cross-layer consistency rules, and anti-pattern catalogs -- and treat single-metric alignment scores as provisional until corroborated by the other lenses; automate detection via scripting where possible (e.g., jArchi over ArchiMate models) to make repeated reassessment practically sustainable.
rationale: The paper proposes an operational alignment evaluation that combines metrics, consistency rules and anti-pattern detection across functional and data dimensions. The CF accurately represents this multi-technique diagnostic approach.

readiness_statement: Organizations achieve IT-business strategic alignment not simply by adopting IT governance (ITG) mechanisms (decision-making structures, formal processes, communication approaches) but only when that adoption translates into genuine organizational commitment to the underlying principles of the ITG framework (e.g., COBIT's five principles: meeting stakeholder needs, end-to-end governance, an integrated evolving framework, a holistic approach, and separating governance from management). Commitment to ITG principles (CCP) fully mediates the relationship between ITG mechanism adoption and strategic alignment -- ITG mechanisms alone do not directly produce alignment.
mechanism: Mechanism adoption can be purely symbolic/instrumental ("following the letter" of governance rules without embracing their spirit/goals), which satisfies structural compliance but does not achieve the values-and-goals-based integration needed for genuine business-IT alignment; only when mechanism adoption is accompanied by felt commitment to the framework's underlying principles does IT become embedded in organizational objectives rather than treated as a separate function.
operationalization_hint: Assess not only whether ITG mechanisms (steering committees, formal processes, communication channels) are formally in place, but whether staff and leadership demonstrate committed endorsement of the governance framework's stated principles (e.g., via a validated CCP-style instrument); a validated CCP measure is provided in this paper and can be adapted to other principles-based frameworks (ISO/IEC 27001, ITIL, NIST, etc.).
rationale: The study reports full mediation of ITG mechanisms by commitment to COBIT principles for strategic alignment and distinguishes symbolic mechanism adoption from substantive commitment. The CF accurately captures the tested mediating relationship.

raw_condition_label: top leadership support spanning board and executive level (not management alone) directly enables both principled governance commitment and strategic alignment
readiness_statement: Achieving IT-business strategic alignment requires support for IT from the full top leadership tier -- including the board of directors, not only C-level executives or IT management -- because top leadership support both strengthens organizational commitment to ITG principles and directly improves strategic alignment. ITG that remains a middle-management affair, without board and executive-level involvement, is unlikely to produce strategic alignment.
mechanism: When top leadership actively participates in IT vision and strategy (rather than passively endorsing it), it diffuses awareness of IT-related values, competencies, and governance principles throughout the firm, secures stakeholder buy-in, and helps overcome organizational resistance to IT-enabled change; because boards sit atop the firm's decision-making and governance hierarchy, their direct involvement (not just senior management's) is what confers legitimacy and centralized momentum to governance initiatives.
operationalization_hint: Measure top leadership support for IT as a construct spanning both board and executive-level participation (not top-management support alone, which is the common but incomplete operationalization in most prior IS research); readiness assessments should specifically check for documented board-level IT engagement, not just CIO/CEO sponsorship.
rationale: The paper defines top leadership support as board and executive participation in IT vision and strategy and reports its links to both commitment and strategic alignment. The CF accurately preserves this broader leadership construct.

A second consideration is that top leadership support of IT (hereafter, “top leadership support”) is
crucial to achieving strategic alignment once ITG mechanisms have been adopted. Importantly, our
conception of top leadership support includes not only top management (C-level executives, such as the
chiefexecutiveofficer,chiefoperatingofficer,andchiefinformationofficer)but alsotheboardofdirectors,
the members of which are crucial stakeholders and decision-makers in the organization’s strategic and
governance structures (Fama & Jensen, 1983; Hillman & Dalziel, 2003) especially concerning ITG
(Andriole, 2009; Benaroch & Chernobai, 2017; Jewer & McKay, 2012). This is a crucial consideration
because even when organizations adopt ITG mechanisms, a lack of top leadership support can hinder
effective ITG and strategic alignment (Ang & Teo, 1997). Even when leaders recognize IT’s value, passive
support may fail to overcome typical organizational user resistance (e.g., Kim & Kankanhalli, 2009).
Support for IT implies that top leadership not only endorses the vision of an IT-enabled organization but

--- PAGE 8 ---
6
also actively participates in IT-related decisions and ITG initiatives. We argue that realizing strategic
alignment requires aligned top leadership support because an organization is shaped by its views and
actions.
Our focus on top leadership support reveals two gaps in how prior research—whether on ITG or IS
more broadly—has used this construct. First, the relationship between top leadership support and
commitment to specific ITG frameworks (such as COBIT), which we argue are necessary for attaining
strategic alignment, has escaped the scrutiny of prior research. Second, top leadership support has been
construed mainly as top-management support for IT (Elbanna, 2013; Kulkarni et al., 2017; Liang et al.,
2007; Liu et al., 2015), yet boards lead corporate governance, including ITG and IT decision-making
(Valentine et al., 2016). Thus, focusing only on top-management support for IT is myopic because it omits
a vital leadership group (the board), which has a critical say in how organizations strategize and operate.
We address this shortcoming by including the board of directors in the firm’s top leadership.

2.3.2. Top-Leadership Support for IT
Based on top-management-support research, we define top leadership support for IT as the effortful
participation and involvement of both the board and executives in the organization’s IT vision and strategy
(Liu et al., 2015; Rai et al., 2009). As such, although top leadership support is not specific to ITG, it is
foundational to and can strengthen an organization’s commitment to ITG principles. Therefore,
commitment to ITG principles concerns the principles-based implementation of ITG. In contrast, top
leadership support concerns the degree of organizational-leader support for IT in general, which is likely to
spill over into support for ITG.
Top leadership plays a crucial role in championing a firm’s ITG principles. Research on organizational
changehasindicatedthatthechangeagents’supportforinitiativesleadsafirm beyondinstrumental-process
change to actual firm-level change (Gondo & Amis, 2013). That is, top leadership championing IT leads
firms beyond the mere adoption of ITG mechanisms—simply an instrumental process change—to
organizational change through a principles-based approach to ITG.
Recent research on board and executive IT expertise has suggested that IT should be supported at the
top levels of leadership because the board and top management jointly establish the ITG ethos and enable
its infusion into every facet of the organization (De Haes et al., 2020a; Haislip et al., 2015; Valentine et al.,
2016). Employee commitment comes only with top leadership support (Wang et al., 2019; Wilkin &
Chenhall,2020).However,suchsupportcanbeelusive.Anorganization’stopleadershipmayincludeboard
members who lack IT backgrounds (Adams et al., 2018), and this lack of technical expertise can further
isolate the IT function and diminish ITG legitimacy. Valentine et al. (2016) evocatively captured the

--- PAGE 14 ---
12
challenge of securing top leadership support:
A majority of boards and senior executives know that technology is critical to their enterprises. However,
only a relatively small number of boards worldwide have made the transition from an almost mono focus
on ﬁnance and legal capability as a proxy for corporate governance to incorporating digital leadership into
the new mix of the board’s structure and capability proﬁle. (p. 577)
It is reasonable to conclude that if top leadership fails to emphasize IT, it may be difficult to achieve
effective ITG. That is why, historically, many firms have lacked broad ITG integration due to the board’s
limited involvement in IT matters (Bart & Turel, 2010; De Haes & Van Grembergen, 2005; Huff et al.,
2006; Jordan & Musson, 2004; Trites, 2004). From an analysis of increases in board IT experience after IT
failure,BenarochandChernobai(2017)concludedthattopleadershipinvolvementcontributesto“ITvalue-
creation through better alignment of investments in IT resource strengths with business priorities” (p. 730).
Top leadership support is foundational to promoting IT-enabled organizational learning and overcoming a
firm’s resistance to IT-enabled change (Wang et al., 2019; Yeow et al., 2018), thus facilitating increased
commitment toestablishedITG principles, such asthose of COBIT. We propose that top leadership support
helps the organization move beyond the mere adoption of ITG mechanisms and toward a more meaningful
implementation of ITG. When firms have top leaders who support IT, they are more likely to “adopt [an
IT] practice substantively, integrating it into their core routines and processes,” thereby facilitating positive
outcomes (Angst et al., 2017, p. 896). Top leadership support, thus, leads to better CCP and strategic
alignment.

H3. CCP will positively influence the organization’s strategic alignment.
3.4. Effect of Top Leadership Support on Strategic Alignment
Building on our problematization, proposing the need for both board and executive support, developed in
Sections 1 and 2.3.2, we now turn to the effect of top leadership support on strategic alignment. In any
organization, when top leadership understands the value of and supports IT, strategic alignment improves
(Ang & Teo, 1997). Formally, when a firm experiences top leadership support for IT, such leadership will
effectively articulate a vision that explains how IT can support the broader business objectives (De Haes et
al., 2020a; Shao et al., 2016). By securing the buy-in and cooperation of organizational stakeholders—
through leadership techniques such as incentives, stimulation, persuasion, and sense-giving—leaders
highlight the need for business objectives to align with a firm’s IT capabilities and vice versa (Awuku-
Gyampoh & Dzisi, 2018; Jenkin et al., 2019; Shao, 2019).
The inference that top leadership support leads to improved strategic alignment also follows from the
strategic management literature, especially strategic leadership theory (Finkelstein et al., 2009). According
to strategic leadership theory, the cognitive values of organizational leaders are reflected in their activities,
in which their leadership techniques facilitate a unified and aligned vision of all business components
(including IT) by promoting cross-firm learning (Vera & Crossan, 2004). To achieve the desired level of
business–IT alignment, top leaders (who support IT) take adequate measures to overcome organizational
resistance (Kim & Kankanhalli, 2009). For example, because Alibaba’s top leadership directed the firm’s
dynamic alignment between IT and business, Alibaba replaced its business strategy of e-commerce with
one of big data and cloud computing (Shao, 2019). In a field study regarding digital strategy adoption,
Yeow et al. (2018) provide similar evidence of the essential role of leadership support. A top leadership
that supports IT continuously monitors IT capabilities and business objectives to steer the alignment of IT
and business objectives (Huygh & Haes, 2020). We thus hypothesize:
H4. Top leadership support in an organization will positively influence the firm’s strategic alignment.

raw_condition_label: commitment to governance principles and top leadership support substitute for, rather than reinforce, each other at high joint levels
readiness_statement: Contrary to the common assumption that stacking multiple enabling conditions produces compounding benefits, this study found that the interaction between commitment to ITG principles (CCP) and top leadership support has a significant NEGATIVE effect on strategic alignment: the highest alignment outcomes occur either from a balanced-but-not-extreme combination of both, or from high CCP paired with lower top leadership support (or vice versa), rather than from both being simultaneously maximized. Both individual relationships were also found to be curvilinear rather than simply linear.
mechanism: A plausible explanation is a substitutive relationship: heavily formalized, principles-based governance frameworks (like COBIT) may constrain leaders' ability to steer nimbly or lead by intuition, so when both principled commitment AND intense leadership steering are simultaneously very high, they may create friction or redundant/conflicting steering inputs rather than reinforcing one another; leaders lacking deep IT expertise may find highly formalized frameworks and highly assertive personal involvement to be competing rather than complementary steering mechanisms.
operationalization_hint: When evaluating governance-readiness conditions, do not assume leadership support and commitment to formal governance principles can simply be maximized independently; assess whether highly formalized governance and strong top-down steering are complementing each other or generating redundant, conflicting control pressure.
rationale: The study models CCP and top-leadership support as distinct influences and reports a non-additive moderation result. The CF appropriately records the finding as a governance-design boundary rather than a universal maximisation rule.

mechanism: Formal processes (continuous monitoring, planning, and capability-development routines) and communication approaches (channels disseminating ITG values and guidelines) directly transmit and reinforce the framework's underlying values across the organization, whereas decision-making structures alone establish authority/roles without necessarily communicating or embedding the values that constitute principled commitment.
operationalization_hint: When designing an ITG rollout intended to build genuine principled commitment (not just structural compliance), prioritize investment in formal governance processes and communication/dissemination channels; do not assume that establishing decision-making bodies (e.g., steering committees) alone will translate into commitment to governance principles.
rationale: The study distinguishes decision structures, formal processes and communication approaches as mechanism types and tests their relationship to commitment to governance principles. The CF accurately reflects the reported differential mechanism result.

Finally, to achieve CCP, an organization should adopt appropriate and effective communication structures.
A firm that adheres to COBIT principles communicates the values, needs, and guidelines in the COBIT
framework across the organization. In discussing how firms can use COBIT to achieve strategic alignment,
Rubino and Vitolla (2014) argued that “a company should elaborate … all that information which
corresponds to its own needs to satisfy the company’s specific business needs” (p. 750, emphasis added).
This highlights the need for a deliberate communication approach to realizing firm-level CCP.
Weproposethat adoptingITGmechanismsisthefirststepindevelopinganorganization’scommitment
to ITG principles. DeSanctis and Poole (1994, p. 127) justify the direction of our hypothesis—ITG
mechanisms precede CCP. That is, the spirit of a system can be fully realized only as part of the
sensemaking process that follows the initial adoption (e.g., Griffith, 1999; Jasperson et al., 2005). Notably,
the spirit of ITG is consensus-oriented (i.e., based on a general commitment to and understanding of the
underlying purpose and values of ITG) rather than regulation-oriented (i.e., oriented toward formal
processes and structures) (Kude et al., 2018) and this consensus is part of the sensemaking process. In
summary, it follows that an organization that adopts ITG mechanisms will be more likely to achieve CCP.
Therefore, we hypothesize:
H1. The adoption of ITG mechanisms in an organization—specifically through (a) ITG decision-
making structures, (b) formal ITG processes, and (c) ITG communication approaches—will positively
influence the firm’s CCP.

raw_condition_label: most existing digital maturity models provide an incomplete picture by addressing either digital-foundation OR transformational-management capabilities, rarely both comprehensively, with the imbalance differing systematically between domain-specific and general models
readiness_statement: Domain-specific models (predominantly manufacturing/Industry 4.0) most strongly emphasize "technology," "digital skills," and "operations & processes," and place significantly more weight on "products & services" and "compliance & security," while general (industry-agnostic) models place much more emphasis on "innovation," "customer insight & experience," and especially "digital culture" and other transformational/soft dimensions (leadership, vision, governance). No examined model comprehensively covers both digital-foundation and transformational-management capabilities at once.
mechanism: Domain-specific models are built to reflect the concrete technological realities of a particular industrial context (e.g., Industry 4.0 manufacturing), which biases their dimension set toward technology and operations, whereas general models must abstract away from industry-specific technical detail and therefore lean on more universally applicable "soft" transformational dimensions -- meaning the choice of model type itself introduces a systematic assessment blind spot.
operationalization_hint: When selecting or adapting a maturity-assessment instrument, explicitly check whether it is domain-specific or general in origin, and supplement it with dimensions from the opposite category (technology/operations detail for general models; culture/leadership/governance depth for domain-specific models) to avoid a one-sided readiness picture.

rationale: The review contrasts domain-specific and general model emphases and concludes that general models more strongly cover transformational capabilities while domain-specific models emphasise technological capabilities. The CF accurately identifies this assessment blind-spot risk.

raw_condition_label: business-model transformation is the most systematically neglected dimension across nearly all existing digital maturity models, despite being central to most academic definitions of digital transformation
readiness_statement: Although prevailing academic definitions of digital transformation explicitly center on developing new digital business models to create and appropriate value, the "business model" maturity area is addressed by only a small minority of the 22 examined models (e.g., just 2 of the synthesized general models explicitly address it), indicating that most existing maturity assessment practice focuses on exploiting digital technology within existing business models rather than exploring digital business-model innovation.
mechanism: Assessing and improving operational/technological digital capabilities is more tractable and less organizationally threatening than reimagining the business model itself, so maturity-model designers (and the organizations using them) default to measuring the former; this creates a systematic blind spot in which an organization can score highly on most maturity dimensions while never having addressed the business-model-level transformation that academic definitions treat as the defining feature of "digital transformation" (as opposed to mere digitization/digitalization).
operationalization_hint: When assessing digital transformation readiness, explicitly verify that a business-model-innovation dimension is included and is not merely inferred from technology or strategy scores, since this is the dimension most likely to be silently absent from off-the-shelf maturity instruments.

rationale: The review shows business model is addressed by only two general models and concludes it is hardly addressed across included maturity models despite transformation relevance. The CF accurately states this systematic omission.

raw_condition_label: cross-industrial digital sensing via technology brokering from outside the firm's own industry and partner network
readiness_statement: Firms build digital sensing capability not only by scanning their own industry and existing partner network but by deliberately searching for and recombining digital solutions already implemented in completely different industries ("technology brokering"), reducing the pressure to invent novel solutions from scratch and lowering the psychological barrier for employees asked to be innovative.
mechanism: Digital innovation does not have to be revolutionary; applying an existing solution from an unrelated industry in a new way is a powerful and more attainable form of sensing than pure invention, but firms have limited natural capacity to search and process knowledge outside their traditional industry boundaries, so this requires a deliberate, dedicated routine (e.g., a consultancy role or cross-industry scanning practice) rather than emerging organically from ordinary business activity.
operationalization_hint: Establish an explicit routine (internal function or external advisor relationship) tasked with identifying digital solutions from unrelated industries and assessing their applicability, rather than relying solely on within-industry competitive scanning.
rationale: The study defines cross-industrial digital sensing as a transformation activity and presents technology brokering as a recognised mechanism for sourcing innovation beyond existing industry knowledge. The CF accurately expresses the proposed sensing routine.

raw_condition_label: inside-out digital infrastructure sensing: firms must first sense and inventory their own existing digital/technical systems before they can identify infrastructure gaps
readiness_statement: A prerequisite sensing capability for digital transformation is internally directed: firms need routines to build an accurate overview of what digital and technical systems already exist within the organization, since lacking this overview is itself an obstacle to transformation -- managers cannot evaluate what new systems or infrastructure are needed, or avoid costly redundant/incompatible builds, without first sensing their own current-state infrastructure.
mechanism: Most digital-sensing capability discussion in the literature is externally oriented (market/competitor/technology scanning), but new digital front-ends or business-model innovations can fail even when well-designed if the firm lacks the underlying infrastructure to support them (e.g., a new digital front-end built for a client that lacked the back-end infrastructure to feed it live data) -- so sensing must also be turned inward before outward-facing digital initiatives can succeed.
operationalization_hint: Before initiating externally-oriented digital sensing/scanning, conduct an internal audit routine establishing an organization-wide inventory of existing digital/technical systems, their current use, and their fitness for future demands.
rationale: The paper reports that absent knowledge of existing internal systems obstructs evaluation of new-system needs, gives an infrastructure-mismatch example, and defines inside-out sensing as routines that evaluate infrastructure demand before searching for new solutions.

raw_condition_label: digital strategy requires semi-continuous, ambidextrous adaptation that balances commitment with flexibility rather than a single fixed plan
readiness_statement: A clear, well-communicated digital strategy with defined business objectives is necessary for digital transformation (without it, employees disagree about what capabilities to develop), but because environmental conditions for digitally transforming firms change rapidly, the strategy and its goals must be semi-continuously readjusted -- alternating between exploitation phases (where resources and priorities are fixed/committed, "semistructures") and exploration phases (where flexibility and new options are considered) -- rather than being set once and executed unchanged.
mechanism: Firms face a dilemma between strategic commitment (needed to realize any given strategy and avoid indecision/paralysis) and strategic flexibility (needed because digital environments and technologies change faster than traditional strategic-planning cycles); resolving this via alternating ambidextrous phases lets a firm exploit committed investments while still periodically re-opening the strategy to newly sensed opportunities, rather than forcing an all-or-nothing choice between rigidity and constant change.
operationalization_hint: Structure digital strategy governance around explicit alternating cycles: periods where digital-project priorities and resource commitments are deliberately fixed (exploitation), interspersed with scheduled strategy-review periods where the digital strategy and objectives are reopened for adjustment based on newly sensed opportunities (exploration).
rationale: The study specifies semi-continuous digital-strategy adaptation, semistructures during exploitation, and re-evaluation during exploration. The CF accurately turns this ambidextrous strategy argument into a governance practice.

readiness_statement: When a digital competence is an essential part of a firm's envisioned digital business model, it should generally be developed internally rather than outsourced, because outsourcing core, high-uncertainty, high-asset-specificity competences creates elevated risk of transactional difficulties and opportunistic behavior by the sourcing partner; outsourcing is more appropriate as a temporary measure in early transformation stages, before the necessity and criticality of a given competence has been determined.
mechanism: Reduced transaction costs favor internalizing competences central to a firm's digital strategy (since high asset specificity and uncertainty otherwise expose the firm to partner opportunism), while competences whose future criticality is not yet clear can reasonably be outsourced provisionally, with the make/outsource decision revisited as the digital strategy and the firm's understanding of its own competence needs matures over time.
operationalization_hint: Maintain an organization-wide (not siloed per-department) inventory of existing internal competences, and explicitly classify each digital capability need as core-to-strategy (internalize) versus provisional/uncertain (outsource pending further clarity), revisiting the classification as the digital strategy develops.
rationale: The source explicitly ties in-house versus outsourcing decisions to competence importance for digital strategy, uncertainty and asset specificity, and recommends ongoing routines to make that decision. The CF accurately represents this boundary-setting rule.

rationale: The qualitative study identifies ecosystem partnerships as an enabler, notes competing interests and limited key partners, and states that strategic management of these relationships conditions the benefit. The CF accurately captures this contingency.

readiness_statement: Faster rates of technology disruption are associated with more aggressive and sophisticated digital transformative capability development, but the same severity of disruption also creates confusion among managers about exactly what capabilities are needed, especially when firms must maintain short-to-medium-term competitiveness without knowing what future market requirements will look like. Moreover, digital transformation itself generates further emerging technologies that fuel additional disruption, creating a continuous, looped change process rather than a discrete transformation event.
mechanism: Technology disruption creates urgency that mobilizes resources and attention, but because disruption is often novel and unprecedented, firms lack established playbooks for responding, so intensifying disruption simultaneously increases both the pressure to act and the uncertainty about which actions will prove correct; because implemented digital transformation itself creates and diffuses new technologies, the disruption that motivated the original transformation is regenerated rather than resolved, meaning firms must treat DTC development as an ongoing capability rather than a one-time project with a defined endpoint.
operationalization_hint: Frame digital-transformation readiness assessments as recurring/cyclical rather than a one-time gate, and explicitly distinguish "urgency to act" from "clarity about what to do," since high-disruption environments can score high on the former while remaining low on the latter.

raw_condition_label: AI/digital-transformation readiness must be assessed across four distinct organizational dimensions (technologies, activities, boundaries, goals) since readiness levels commonly diverge sharply across them
readiness_statement: Organizational readiness to deploy transformative technologies like AI cannot be captured by a single readiness score; it must be assessed separately across at least four dimensions -- technologies (value-adding potential of the current/future technology portfolio), activities (which organizational activities the technology supports), boundaries (whether organizational boundaries with customers/partners are being reshaped), and goals (whether the technology supports attainment of organizational goals/identity) -- because readiness commonly diverges sharply across these dimensions (e.g., high technology readiness but zero goal-alignment readiness in the illustrated case).
mechanism: Treating "AI readiness" or "digital readiness" as a single undifferentiated score masks exactly where the bottleneck to further transformation lies; in the illustrated case, an organization rated itself highly on current technology capability but scored zero on goal-alignment, revealing that its actual constraint on further digital transformation was not technological capability at all but the absence of any goal-level rationale for deploying the technology further.
operationalization_hint: Use a structured, multi-dimensional self-assessment instrument (e.g., a 0-4 scored questionnaire completed by a cross-functional management workshop) scoring current AND future/planned capability separately across technologies, activities, boundaries, and goals, and visualize the four scores together (e.g., a radar/scorecard) rather than aggregating into one composite readiness index.
rationale: The AI readiness framework explicitly assesses technologies, activities, boundaries and goals and provides a workshop scorecard to reveal divergent readiness across them. The CF accurately describes the four-dimensional instrument.

raw_condition_label: digital maturity fully mediates the effect of both digital orientation and digital intensity on financial success -- neither antecedent alone drives financial performance
readiness_statement: Across 284 large Finnish companies (secondary data: annual-report content analysis plus audited financial statements), digital orientation (commitment/openness to digital technology) and digital intensity (breadth of areas digitalized) show no significant direct effect on financial success (net profit or operating profit); their effects on financial performance are realized entirely through digital maturity (systematic, ongoing capability to adapt to digital change), which fully mediates both relationships.
mechanism: Openness/commitment to digital technology and breadth of digital initiatives are necessary inputs, but without the systematic organizational capability to translate them into sustained, coordinated adaptation (digital maturity), they do not convert into financial outcomes; digital maturity is the capability layer that actually captures value from orientation and intensity.
operationalization_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness for financial-performance purposes, do not treat digital orientation (stated commitment) or digital intensity (breadth of digital initiatives) as sufficient readiness indicators on their own; require evidence of digital maturity (systematic, sustained adaptation capability, e.g. per Westerman et al.'s four-level model) before expecting financial returns.
rationale: The quantitative study explicitly evaluates full mediation of orientation and intensity by digital maturity in relation to financial success. The CF accurately reports the tested mediation result and its performance boundary.

readiness_statement: Digital intensity significantly and negatively moderates the relationship between digital orientation and financial success (both net profit and operating profit): the wider the breadth of areas a company digitalizes simultaneously, the weaker the financial return from its digital commitment/orientation.
mechanism: High digital intensity across many operational areas increases the number of engaged actors and organizational complexity, which can jeopardize managerial control over the business even when digital commitment (orientation) is strong; without a correspondingly high level of digital maturity to manage this complexity, spreading digital effort thin across many domains erodes rather than reinforces the financial payoff of digital commitment.
operationalization_hint: When planning digital transformation scope, deliberately weigh breadth (number of areas digitalized) against organizational capacity to maintain control and coherence; flag high-breadth digital initiatives that are not matched by a correspondingly high digital-maturity level as a financial-performance risk, not an automatic strength.
rationale: The regression study defines digital intensity as breadth across operational areas and reports that it negatively moderates the digital-orientation to financial-success relation. Its discussion links broad intensity to control, actor, and complexity challenges where maturity is insufficient. The CF faithfully reflects this qualified financial-performance finding.

title: Mastering the digital transformation through organizational capabilities: A conceptual framework

raw_condition_label: organizational capability development for digital transformation must be sequenced according to which capability theme has the highest relevance at each process stage (sensing, seizing, transforming), rather than pursued uniformly
readiness_statement: Across seven organizational-capability themes (Strategy & Ecosystem, Innovation Thinking, DT Technologies, Data, Operations, Organizational Design, DT Leadership), the relative importance of each theme shifts systematically across Teece's sensing, seizing, and transforming mechanisms: Innovation Thinking and DT Technologies capabilities carry the highest relevance during sensing (external scanning, technology/customer-need awareness); Strategy & Ecosystem, Operations, and Data capabilities peak during seizing (partner/network management, internal process improvement, data protection and exploitation); and Organizational Design and DT Leadership capabilities carry the highest relevance during transforming (structural adaptation, culture, incentives).
mechanism: Because organizational capabilities are the concrete, actionable substrate of the abstract sensing/seizing/transforming dynamic-capability mechanisms, and because the relative importance of each of the seven capability themes shifts systematically across the three mechanisms, organizations that try to develop all seven capability themes simultaneously and uniformly misallocate scarce transformation resources; sequencing capability investment to match the currently active mechanism is more resource-efficient than a flat, undifferentiated capability-development agenda.
operationalization_hint: Use a digital maturity assessment first to identify which of the three mechanism-stages (sensing/seizing/transforming) the organization is currently in, then prioritize capability-development investment in the 2-3 capability themes empirically shown to carry the highest relative relevance for that specific stage, rather than pursuing all seven themes at once.
rationale: The conceptual review structures dynamic capabilities as sensing, seizing and transforming, identifies seven themes, and calculates their stage-relative relevance. The CF accurately states the proposed sequencing logic.

title: Enlightening the dynamic capabilities of design thinking in fostering digital transformation

authors: Magistretti, S.; Pham, C.T.A.; Dell'Era, C.
raw_condition_label: five design-thinking dynamic capabilities (extending, debating, cropping, interpreting, recombining) enable human-centered digital transformation by integrating technological and human perspectives
readiness_statement: Organizations pursuing digital transformation benefit from five specific design-thinking-rooted dynamic capabilities that translate ambiguous technological challenges into human-valued opportunities: (1) extending -- enlarging the shared knowledge base through close collaboration with diverse internal/external stakeholders; (2) debating -- juxtaposing digital/technological and human perspectives via critical questioning to reframe the challenge; (3) cropping -- selecting/retaining only the technological requirements and solution alternatives relevant to actual user needs, rather than being driven purely by data or technical functionality; (4) interpreting -- adopting different perceptual frames (e.g., distinct user archetypes/personas) to uncover new opportunities in the technology; and (5) recombining -- synthesizing technological and human/socio-cultural knowledge into a holistic solution framing.
mechanism: Standard dynamic-capability treatments of digital transformation (sensing/seizing/reconfiguring) are technology- and strategy-centered and risk producing digital solutions that are technically feasible but not meaningful or adopted by end users; design-thinking-rooted capabilities counterbalance this by embedding continuous empathizing, reframing, and synthesis activities throughout the technology-adoption process, ensuring that the opportunities provided by digital technologies result from harmonization with people's lives rather than treating the technology itself as the solution.
operationalization_hint: When running a digital-transformation initiative, explicitly assign process steps/roles for each of the five capabilities (e.g., structured stakeholder-extension sessions, dedicated debate/critique sessions contrasting technical vs. human framings, criteria-based cropping of requirements against user archetypes, and recombination workshops synthesizing technical and human insights) rather than relying on a generic "user research" phase alone.
rationale: The multiple-case study defines the five design-thinking dynamic capabilities and positions them as a human-centred complement to technology-focused digital transformation. The CF accurately represents the proposed capability set.

readiness_statement: In all four cases, the design-thinking dynamic capabilities needed for human-centered digital transformation were built and exercised through a close, iterative collaboration between the transforming organization and an external consulting/design partner, who mediated between technical/business stakeholders and end users; the consulting relationship itself was the vehicle through which extending, debating, cropping, interpreting, and recombining capabilities were enacted.

rationale: The multiple-case design describes external design-oriented collaboration as the context in which the dynamic capabilities were exercised. The CF appropriately presents external mediation as a possible vehicle, not a universal prerequisite.

readiness_statement: A TISM-based hierarchical analysis of four SME digital-transformation factors -- Digital Awareness, Digital Strategy and Roadmap, Digital Adoption and Implementation, and Digital Transformation Continuous Improvement -- found all four factors mutually reachable and effectively at the same hierarchical level due to circular feedback relationships (continuous improvement feeds back into awareness; implementation experience feeds back into strategy), rather than forming a strict linear stage sequence.
mechanism: Because implementation reveals new information that must immediately revise strategy, and because continuous-improvement learning reshapes organizational digital awareness, treating digital transformation as a one-time, front-to-back linear project (awareness then strategy then adoption then done) misrepresents its actual dynamics; the cyclical structure lets organizations respond to emerging challenges or opportunities without waiting for a complete transformation cycle to finish.
operationalization_hint: When designing an SME digital-transformation roadmap, build in explicit feedback loops (e.g., scheduled strategy-revision checkpoints informed by implementation learnings, and awareness-refresh activities informed by continuous-improvement insights) rather than treating awareness-building, strategizing, and implementation as one-off sequential phases.
rationale: The TISM analysis identifies circular feedback among awareness, strategy, implementation, and continuous improvement; it explains immediate strategy adjustment from implementation feedback and presents DASAT as a cyclical SME transformation approach rather than a linear sequence.

readiness_statement: Strong digital awareness and literacy established early in a transformation directly reduces employee resistance during the later digital-adoption-and-implementation stage, because employees who understand digital transformation's purpose and benefits are less likely to fear job displacement; under-investing in the awareness stage is expected to manifest predictably as resistance problems later, rather than resistance being an independent, unrelated barrier.

operationalization_hint: Treat awareness-building as an upstream change-management control: assess whether employees receive early explanation of the transformation's purpose, expected benefits, and role implications, and treat weak digital literacy or weak awareness communication as a predictor of later implementation resistance rather than as a separate downstream surprise.
rationale: The DASAT framework explicitly identifies digital literacy as reducing resistance and directly links early digital awareness to lower implementation resistance and job-loss concerns. The CF accurately states the framework relationship.

4.1. Digital Awareness
The first step in digital transformation is digital awareness, which involves under-
standing the available technologies—such as cloud computing, AI, automation, and digital
payments—and recognizing their potential impact on business operations. Firms cannot
manage what they do not know. This is aligned with Garzoni et al.’s (2020) digital aware-
ness level and aligns Teece’s (2007) concept of “sensing” and Rashidirad and Salimian’s
(2020) “sensing and learning” framework, where organizations scan, search, and explore
opportunities and threats across technologies and markets, and is aligned with the research
of Christofi et al. (2024).
One of the major barriers for SMEs is the lack of digital skills, including both technical
expertise and the digital mindset required for transformation (Moeuf et al., 2018; Pfister
& Lehmann, 2023; Schönberger, 2023; Solberg et al., 2020). Without these skills, SMEs
fail to recognize the benefits, risks, and integration of digital technologies often leading
to skepticism and resistance to change (Klein & Todesco, 2021; Skouloudis et al., 2020).
Business success relies on integrating technical knowledge with market knowledge. SMEs
with betterdigital awareness can identify relevanttechnologies, assess their strategic fit, and
develop realistic implementation plans based on a clearer understanding of technological
possibilities and limitations.
Digital Awareness, Literacy, and Inclusion
This stage ensures SMEs understand how digitalization can support their business.
Digital literacy minimizes resistance to change and helps firms grasp the potential benefits
(Pfister & Lehmann, 2023; Radicic & Petković, 2023; Sousa-Zomer et al., 2020). Once SMEs

A major barrier is employee resistance, often stemming from fear of job displacement
and reluctance to abandon familiar processes. Employees are a key resource in realizing
the benefits of digital transformation, which include cost reduction, improved efficiency,
enhanced performance, and increased revenue and company growth. This highlights the
cyclical nature of the DASAT framework, as strong digital awareness from the first step
directly reduces implementation resistance. When employees understand digital trans-
formation’s purpose and benefits, they are less likely to fear job loss. Management must

title: Building and development of an organizational competence for digital transformation in SMEs

authors: González-Varona, J.M.; López-Paredes, A.; Poza, D.; Acebes, F.
raw_condition_label: SME digital transformation competence must be organized as a resource-to-core-competence hierarchy adapted to SME resource constraints, not borrowed directly from large-firm maturity models
readiness_statement: SMEs need an organizational-competence hierarchy for digital transformation adapted to their specific constraints (limited resources, limited specialization capability) rather than directly applying digital maturity models designed for large companies (e.g., MIT/Capgemini, McKinsey, Forrester); the proposed model organizes competence at four levels -- resources (physical/human/organizational), capabilities (functional-level ability to exploit resources), competencies (multifunctional integration of capabilities spanning governance, organizational alignment, culture, technology, and employees), and core competencies -- with digital maturity progress as the outcome.
mechanism: Large-firm digital maturity models assume specialization capacity and resource slack that SMEs typically lack, so directly applying them risks setting unattainable or poorly-prioritized capability targets; a hierarchy that explicitly starts from the SME's actual resource base and builds up through functional capabilities before multifunctional competencies gives SME managers a more realistic, sequenced path to digital maturity.
operationalization_hint: When assessing SME digital-transformation readiness, start from an inventory of actual physical/human/organizational resources rather than benchmarking directly against large-firm maturity-model stage descriptions; build capability-development plans bottom-up (resources to functional capabilities to cross-functional competencies) rather than top-down.
rationale: The SME framework is explicitly organised as a resource, capability, competence and core-competence hierarchy. The CF accurately presents the resulting bottom-up assessment logic for resource-constrained firms.

raw_condition_label: information culture -- open flow of relevant, high-quality information across all employees -- is a distinct competence element enabling SME digital transformation
readiness_statement: A distinct "information culture" -- the socially shared patterns of behavior, norms and values defining the importance and use of information in an organization, requiring information to flow openly and be relevant/high-quality across all SME employees -- emerged from expert interviews and was added as a new element within the organizational-culture competence dimension, distinct from other culture types (results-oriented, rule-following, relationship-oriented, risk-taking).
mechanism: Because SMEs typically have flatter, less specialized structures than large firms, digital-transformation-relevant information cannot rely on formal specialist channels alone; it must flow openly and be actively valued across the whole workforce for decisions and digital-capability development to be well-informed, making information culture a load-bearing (not merely supporting) element of digital-transformation competence in this context.
operationalization_hint: Assess whether SME employees across all roles (not just IT/management) have open, quality-controlled access to digitalization-relevant information, and whether the organization's culture actively values and rewards sharing such information, as a distinct readiness sub-check separate from general "collaborative culture" measures.
rationale: The paper reports interview evidence that information should flow among all SME employees and be relevant and high quality, defines information culture, and adds it as a competence element in the authors' improved OCDT model. The CF remains appropriately bounded to the SME/OCDT context.

spans.source_excerpt:
An important factor identified by three of the interviewees was the need for an information culture "it is necessary
that information flows between all employees of the SME. In addition, the information must be relevant and of
good quality".
The information culture can be define as "the socially shared patterns of behavior, norms and values that define
the importance and use of information in an organization" (Choo, Bergeron, Detlor & Heaton, 2008; Choo,
Furness, Paquette, Van Den Berg Detlor, Bergeron et al., 2006).
We can identify four types of information culture in an organization: the results-oriented culture in which the aim is
to make it easier for the organization to compete and succeed in the market, the culture of following rules that
allows internal operations to be controlled and rules and policies to be strengthened, the culture of the relationship
that is managed to encourage team spirit and belonging, internal communication and participation, and finally, the
risk-taking culture, in which information is managed to encourage innovation, creativity and the generation of new
ideas. The information culture of an organization is related to organizational effectiveness (Choo, 2013).
In research by Marchand, Kettinger and Rollins (2001), with a survey of rather than thousand senior managers, they
identified three "information capabilities" that an organization needs to develop to improve its performance:
information technology practices, management practices of information and information behaviors and values.
Therefore, an open information culture involving the exchange of information should be particularly important for
the development of an OCDT and that is why in our improved model we included “information” as a new element
of competence within the culture dimension.

readiness_statement: Across a large sample of 400 heterogeneous Italian museums, an organization-wide Digital Readiness Index (DRI) computed as a weighted composite of five dimensions -- people (digital skills), technology (adoption, data analytics, infrastructure), process (front/back office digitization), customer (digital engagement channels), and strategy and investment -- averaged only 0.35/1, with People (0.29) and Process (0.21) scoring as the weakest dimensions, while Technology (0.40), Customer (0.38), and Strategy and Investment (0.38) scored moderately higher.
mechanism: In resource-constrained, historically non-digital organizations, staff digital skills and internal process digitization lag furthest behind because they require deep, sustained investment in human capital and back-office system overhauls, whereas technology adoption and customer-facing digital channels (e.g., social media presence) can be added more incrementally and visibly without requiring the same depth of internal capability change -- meaning readiness gaps concentrate disproportionately in the least visible, hardest-to-fix dimensions.
operationalization_hint: When assessing organizational digital readiness, compute and report per-dimension scores (not just a single composite index) so that hidden bottlenecks in people/digital-skills and back-office process digitization are not masked by more visible progress in technology adoption or customer-facing channels; benchmark against sector peers per dimension to prioritize investment.
rationale: The cultural-institutions framework defines a multidimensional Digital Readiness Index and quantifies internal process digitisation and associated readiness dimensions. The CF correctly emphasises reporting dimensions separately as well as the composite.

readiness_statement: Despite extensive literatures on "e-readiness" (278 Web of Science articles, ~74% of the combined readiness literature) and "digital readiness" (91 articles, ~24%) as pre-transformation assessment constructs, articles specifically addressing organizational readiness for digital transformation represent only about 2% of the combined literature (7-8 articles identified via systematic PRISMA-based search across 2004-2022), despite digital transformation itself having a vastly larger literature base (5,007 articles) -- revealing a quotable gap between how much is written about "being digital-ready" in general versus specifically "being ready to undertake a transformation."
mechanism: E-readiness and digital readiness research trace back to national/institutional digital-divide assessment (public policy, e-government, e-commerce adoption) and have accumulated decades of measurement tradition, whereas organizational readiness specifically for the more radical, business-model-level change implied by "transformation" is a recent (post-2017), still-nascent research thread that has not yet benefited from the same accumulated conceptual and empirical development.
operationalization_hint: When designing or evaluating a readiness-assessment instrument for RQ1 purposes, treat off-the-shelf "e-readiness" or general "digital readiness" instruments with caution, since they were developed for a different (broader, less transformation-specific) construct and may not adequately capture the conditions specific to enterprise-scale transformation readiness.

raw_condition_label: digital maturity models must accommodate a "Level 0 (incomplete)" starting point for organizations in developing economies that have not yet reached the conventional baseline assumed by most maturity frameworks
readiness_statement: Adapting the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) framework for organizational digital transformation readiness, this study explicitly adds a "Level 0 (incomplete)" starting point -- where processes are unpredictable, poorly controlled, and management is reactive with inconsistent performance -- below the conventional "Level 1 (initial)" baseline that most existing digital maturity models assume as the starting point, specifically to account for businesses in developing-country contexts that have not yet reached even that baseline.
mechanism: Most published digital maturity models (e.g., standard CMMI-based frameworks) implicitly assume organizations start at "Level 1" with at least an initial, ad hoc approach already in place; but many businesses in developing-economy contexts have not yet reached even this baseline, so readiness models transplanted directly from developed-economy contexts systematically fail to differentiate or represent the actual starting conditions of organizations in less digitally mature economies.
operationalization_hint: When applying a maturity-based readiness assessment in a developing-economy or otherwise under-digitized context, explicitly include a "no/incomplete process" floor level below the standard "initial" level, rather than assuming all assessed organizations have at least reached a baseline of ad hoc digital practice.
rationale: The ODTR study explicitly introduces Level 0 for developing-country organisations that do not meet conventional Level 1 assumptions. The CF accurately records this contextual maturity-floor requirement.

raw_condition_label: digital transformation readiness operates in a cyclical, three-level system (competitive environment, organization, organizational dimensions) in which successful transformation reshapes the very competitive environment that originally necessitated it
readiness_statement: The proposed ODTR framework structures readiness across three interacting levels: the macro-level competitive environment (market and context), the meso-level organization (assessed through the five ODTR dimensions), and the micro-level dimensions themselves (technological resources, business processes, management capability, human capability, corporate culture, which interact without a fixed hierarchy). Critically, the framework is cyclical rather than linear: once digital transformation is achieved, it feeds back to impact both the organization and the competitive environment in which it operates, meaning readiness is not a one-time gate but an input to a recurring loop.
mechanism: Because digital transformation changes an organization's capabilities and market behavior, and because competitors and the broader market simultaneously adapt to the resulting shifts, the competitive environment that originally created pressure for transformation is itself altered by the transformation, which in turn changes the readiness requirements for the organization's next transformation cycle -- so treating "readiness" as a fixed target state to reach once misrepresents the ongoing, environment-reshaping nature of the process.
operationalization_hint: When designing a readiness-assessment governance artifact, build in a recurring reassessment trigger tied to competitive-environment monitoring (not just internal capability tracking), since a successful transformation changes the environment against which future readiness must be judged.

readiness_statement: Across interviews spanning five South African industries, the successful roll-out of digital transformation was found to be driven predominantly by people elements (organisational culture, workforce skills/training, employee well-being); it is critical for organisations to invest in technological infrastructure only once the people elements have been addressed, since people are the drivers of technology implementation rather than a downstream afterthought.

rationale: The study's abstract and conclusion identify culture, skills, engagement and well-being as people elements driving transformation and state that technological infrastructure should be invested in once these people elements are addressed.

readiness_statement: Digital transformation initiatives generate identifiable technostress risks for employees -- job security fears from automation (e.g., in mining, where advanced analytics threatens to reduce headcount), techno-invasion as remote-work technologies blur personal/professional boundaries, and techno-insecurity from rapidly evolving skill requirements -- which organisations must actively identify, monitor, and mitigate as a distinct, ongoing risk-management track throughout the transformation rather than treating employee stress as an unavoidable side effect of change.

operationalization_hint: Establish an ongoing technostress-monitoring track parallel to the technical rollout: identify likely technostressors (overload, invasion, insecurity, complexity) specific to the initiative, evaluate situational factors and design targeted interventions (e.g., structured training, clearer job-security communication, boundary-setting norms for remote work), and monitor employee strain levels continuously, especially during peak transformation activity.
rationale: The qualitative framework identifies job security and techno-invasion as technostress sources, calls for leadership measures, and recommends identifying and monitoring technostressors. The CF accurately frames technostress as an ongoing wellbeing risk.
