raw_condition_label: employee negative emotional reactions to digital transformation are frequently misattributed as resistance to change, when they more often reflect protest against organizational inaction rather than resistance to the technology itself
readiness_statement: Across a large-sample survey (135 respondents, 44 municipalities) and interview study (24 respondents, 13 municipalities) on municipal digital transformation, sentiment analysis of interview transcripts found negative emotions (fear, frustration, anger) nearly balanced with positive emotions (41% vs. 49%), but qualitative follow-up discussion revealed that most of these negative emotions did not reflect employee resistance to change/technology itself; instead, they reflected dissatisfaction and protest at the organization's failure to act (absence of strategy, structure, or support for digital transformation) -- a fundamentally different diagnosis with different remediation implications.
mechanism: Coding raw sentiment as "negative = resistance to change" without deeper qualitative interpretation risks misdiagnosing the actual barrier; in this study, employees expressing anger or frustration were often protesting the lack of organizational digital-transformation activity (no structure, no strategic plan, no training) rather than opposing change itself -- meaning organizations that interpret negative employee sentiment as resistance-to-technology and respond with change-management/persuasion tactics may be addressing the wrong problem, when the actual fix needed is organizational action (providing structure, strategy, and resources), not overcoming employee reluctance.
operationalization_hint: When negative employee sentiment toward digital transformation is detected, do not automatically categorize it as "resistance to change"; use follow-up qualitative probing to correctly diagnose whether the barrier is organizational inaction or genuine resistance, since the appropriate remediation differs substantially between the two.
rationale: The municipal study reports near-balanced positive and negative sentiment and, after discussion with respondents, finds that most negative emotions reflected protest at unaddressed organisational conditions rather than resistance to change itself. It explicitly warns that sentiment alone would misinterpret the behaviour.

line) clearly varies from question to question from its minimum in Q4 to
its maximum in Q5.
Q1 on the definition and vision of digital transformation elicits
contrasting reactions between hope and incomprehension. For instance,
a respondent indicated that:
“Be able to look up all the information live there. Cool! It’s ideal but
hard to pinpoint what’s really important in the face of total disarray
in our business units.”
Q2 on changing the regulations, as well as Q4 on setting up a digital
transformation support structure, provoked much more negative re­
actions that tended towards frustration and anger.
There is a meeting point of feelings in Q3 where respondents express
opposite emotions. On the one hand, there is satisfaction with the ac­
celeration of digital transformation generated by the pandemic. On the
other hand, there was dissatisfaction, as processes and practices were
slightly transformed. Moreover, digital transformation is done in a
random, unstructured and unfederated way by the municipality.
Q5, on the impact of digital transformation on employees and
citizens, elicits many mixed responses, seemingly dominated by age-
related fear.
“There are colleagues who are lost, it stresses them out, especially
those close to retirement. I have a few colleagues who have rushed
into retirement because they are afraid.”
However, after reflection and discussion with the respondents, most
of these negative emotions are not a form of resistance to change. It
has more todo with dissatisfaction withthe current situation because
it is not being addressed:
“…especially, it’s not their role at all, and worse, nobody’s role.”
Therefore, it is a form of municipal employee protest that can really
push towards positive change.
The analysis of the feelings reveals several findings and conclusions.
This analysis allowed us to gain a better understanding of the human
being and the issues at stake in the digital transformation. We noted the
variation in emotions and reactions from one question to another. We
wanted to better understand why frustration and anger is a form of
resistance to change. After reflection and discussion with the re­
spondents, most of these negative emotions are not a form of resistance
to change.
It has more to do with dissatisfaction with the current situation, as it
is not being addressed. Therefore, it is a form of protest by city em­
ployees that can really push for positive change. Sometimes this anger is
related to the administrative burden in the municipal environment,
which has an impact on the behavior of the employees. Time is therefore
an indicator to be taken into consideration to keep employees engaged
and motivated. On the one hand, there is contentment with the accel­
eration of the digital transformation generated by the pandemic. On the
other hand, there is dissatisfaction, as processes and practices are
slightly transformed. In addition, the digital transformation is done in a
random, unstructured and unfederated way by the city. Without the
analysis of feelings, we would never have known the true interpretation
of the respondents’ behavior. Sentences expressing anger would have
been associated with resistance to change, contrary to reality. Also, the
municipal organization must pay attention to its employees and their
behaviours and concerns. Finally, it is the employees who will apply the
activities mentioned in the framework developed in the article.

mechanism: In organizations undertaking piecemeal, haphazard digitization (digitizing individual data sets without an overarching data-governance practice), the resulting data remains siloed, unusable for cross-departmental decision-making, and disconnected from asset-lifecycle planning -- so even where individual digitization initiatives exist, the absence of systematic data management (not lack of strategy or culture per se) becomes the single largest practical obstacle to realizing value from digital transformation.
operationalization_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness in asset-heavy, siloed public-sector organizations, prioritize diagnosing data-management practices (data governance, cross-departmental sharing mechanisms, dedicated data teams) as the highest-leverage barrier to address, rather than assuming strategy or culture gaps are the primary bottleneck.
rationale: The validated municipal barrier framework records absence of data management as 90 references or 18% of coded barriers. The CF accurately reports this context-specific quantitative predominance.

mechanism: Maturity models are typically designed around descriptive stage/level frameworks (e.g., "beginner" to "advanced"), which are useful for benchmarking position but do not by themselves reveal the causal obstacles (financial, technical, human, regulatory) responsible for an organization's current position, so organizations using only a maturity score lack actionable diagnostic guidance on where to intervene.
operationalization_hint: Supplement any digital maturity assessment model with a dedicated barrier-evaluation instrument (e.g., a structured questionnaire scoring specific barrier areas as no/local/enterprise-wide barrier) rather than relying on a maturity score alone to guide intervention priorities.
rationale: The high-technology manufacturing paper reviews 18 maturity models and distinguishes maturity-position assessment from direct barrier diagnosis. The CF accurately identifies this diagnostic limitation.

readiness_statement: Validated by manufacturing industry representatives, a barrier taxonomy for high-technology manufacturing digital transformation includes not only common areas (IT infrastructure, existing systems, financial resources, qualified specialists, training, digital policy) but also two less commonly captured areas: "diverse IT maturity of production cooperation participants" (a barrier when key partners/suppliers cannot exchange information in the required digital format) and "insufficient elaboration of secure-access channels/regulatory framework for limited-access information" (a barrier specific to industries handling sensitive, export-controlled, or state-secret information).
mechanism: In defense-adjacent, high-technology, or otherwise regulated manufacturing sectors, digital transformation is constrained not only by internal organizational readiness but by the digital maturity of the broader industrial cooperation network (since production increasingly depends on multi-party digital information exchange) and by legal/security requirements governing how sensitive information may be transferred digitally -- barriers that are largely absent from general-purpose digital maturity frameworks designed for less regulated or single-organization contexts.
operationalization_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness in regulated, high-technology, or supply-chain-dependent manufacturing contexts, explicitly add barrier-assessment items for (a) the digital-information-exchange maturity of key external cooperation partners and (b) the adequacy of secure/limited-access information-transfer channels and their supporting regulatory documentation.
rationale: The validated manufacturing taxonomy includes diverse IT maturity of production-cooperation participants and a regulatory framework among the barrier areas. The CF accurately identifies these regulated ecosystem contingencies.

raw_condition_label: organizational agility drives SME digital transformation success primarily indirectly through digital capability, which has a substantially stronger direct effect on transformation performance than agility itself
readiness_statement: Across 359 Chinese technology-based SMEs, organizational agility strongly predicts digital capability (beta=0.551, the strongest path in the model), and digital capability has a substantially stronger direct effect on digital innovation performance (beta=0.269) than organizational agility's own direct effect (beta=0.137); digital capability was also confirmed as a significant mediator of the agility-to-transformation relationship (indirect beta=0.148). This indicates agility is a necessary organizational-level precondition, but its practical payoff for transformation success is realized mainly by being converted into digital capability, not through agility's direct effect alone.
mechanism: Organizational agility (rapid responsiveness, adaptability to market/customer change) creates the organizational conditions under which digital capability can be built and exercised, but agility alone -- the ability to react quickly -- does not by itself constitute the capacity to sense, operationalize, and integrate digital technology; digital capability is the more proximate, integrative mechanism that actually converts organizational responsiveness into transformation outcomes, which is why its direct effect on performance outweighs agility's.
operationalization_hint: When assessing SME digital-transformation readiness, do not treat organizational agility as a sufficient condition on its own; verify that agility is being actively converted into digital capability (sensing, operationalizing, and integrating digital technology) rather than assuming rapid responsiveness alone will produce transformation success.
rationale: The SME structural-model results show agility's direct path, digital capability's stronger direct path, and the significant indirect agility-to-performance effect through digital capability. The CF accurately reports the mediation pattern.

rationale: The SME study models top-management support as a moderation condition alongside agility and digital capability. The CF appropriately represents its role as a context-specific, comparatively modest enabling condition.

raw_condition_label: the "process" dimension (not people or technology) is frequently the hardest digital-transformation readiness dimension to improve, due to production-system rigidity and replicability constraints
readiness_statement: Across 36 surveyed Italian companies, the "people" and "technology" dimensions scored as the most digitally mature/performing dimensions, while "process" -- the ability of business processes to be repeatably and flexibly executed regardless of who performs them -- was identified as the dimension where digital transformation was hardest to implement, attributed to the inherent rigidity and low replicability of existing production systems.
mechanism: Digital tools can be acquired (technology) and staff can be trained or hired with relevant skills (people) comparatively quickly, but re-engineering established production processes to be standardized, repeatable, and flexible enough to support digital transformation requires restructuring deeply embedded operational routines and physical/organizational workflows, which resist change far more than technology procurement or individual skill-building.
operationalization_hint: When diagnosing digital-transformation readiness bottlenecks, do not assume people/culture is always the limiting dimension; explicitly assess process rigidity and replicability as a potentially distinct and harder-to-shift bottleneck, particularly in production/manufacturing-heavy contexts.
rationale: The production-systems study compares people, technology and process readiness dimensions across surveyed firms. The CF appropriately records process rigidity as a context-specific bottleneck rather than a universal ranking.

raw_condition_label: full digital-transformation readiness (the highest maturity level) was not achieved by any company in a 36-company, four-sector sample, and readiness scales with firm size, turnover, and percentage of turnover invested in digital technologies
readiness_statement: Across 36 companies spanning four industrial sectors, zero companies reached the highest "Digital Transformation" readiness level (level 5 of 5); readiness instead clustered at "Not existent" (24.6%), "Basic digital operation" (21.5%), "Advanced digital operation" (30.7%), and "Digital integration" (23.2%). Readiness scaled in a graded, dose-response manner with firm size (small vs. medium vs. large), annual turnover, and the percentage of turnover invested in digital technologies/IT/innovation (companies investing over 5% of turnover scored roughly 3x higher average readiness than those investing less).
mechanism: Achieving full digital transformation requires simultaneous, sustained maturity across people, process, technology, and innovation dimensions, which is disproportionately difficult for smaller or less digitally-invested firms that lack the resource base to advance all four dimensions in parallel; larger firms and those investing a higher share of turnover in digital technologies can sustain broader, more parallel capability development, producing the observed graded relationship between resource commitment/scale and readiness level.
operationalization_hint: When benchmarking a firm's digital-transformation readiness, calibrate expectations against firm size and digital-investment intensity (e.g., percentage of turnover) rather than against an absolute "fully transformed" target, since even well-resourced firms in a broad cross-sector sample rarely if ever reach complete transformation.
rationale: The cross-sector production-systems survey assesses digital readiness relative to firm resources and investment capacity. The CF accurately expresses that its complete-transformation result is a sample-specific benchmark rather than a universal ceiling.

authors: Dang-Pham, D.; Hoang, A.-P.; Vo, D.-T.; Kautz, K.
raw_condition_label: decomposing large-scale digital transformation into small, quick-win projects resolving cross-functional pain points (identified via structured, mandatory cross-departmental workshops) builds transformation momentum incrementally
readiness_statement: Rather than pursuing "big-bang" disruption, successful large-scale digital transformation can be decomposed into a repeatable six-step cycle (discover improvement potential, analyse current work, generate ideas, develop/implement, evaluate) applied to small, cross-functional "pain points" identified through regular, mandatory workshops attended by managers from all departments, with each resulting project capped at strict time (e.g., 6-month) and evaluation (feasibility, urgency, strategic value) criteria; visible, fast wins from these small projects build employee morale and management trust, which in turn increases participation in subsequent transformation initiatives.
mechanism: Framing digital transformation as one large, uncertain, resource-intensive program tends to make managers hesitant or resistant, especially in SMEs and even large enterprises facing scope-creep risk; by contrast, decomposing the transformation into small, time-boxed projects that solve problems employees actually experience day-to-day (rather than top-down mandated initiatives) produces fast, visible, and attributable wins, and these visible successes create a self-reinforcing cycle of trust and morale that lowers resistance to the next round of change.
operationalization_hint: Structure digital-transformation programs as a repeating cycle of short (e.g., 3-6 month), strictly time-boxed projects targeting specific, employee-identified cross-functional pain points -- prioritized by feasibility, urgency, and strategic value -- rather than as a single large multi-year initiative, and use regular mandatory cross-departmental workshops as the mechanism for continuously surfacing new pain points.
page_or_section: Sections 4, 4.3, 5.2 (Digital Kaizen process model; MyFPT and AkaLink cases)
rationale: Digital Kaizen explicitly uses mandatory workshops to identify cross-functional pain points, ranks solutions against strategic criteria, and promotes a continuous improvement strategy. The CF accurately converts this into a repeatable small-project approach.

raw_condition_label: even benchmark "digital pioneer" enterprises show weaker professional-management and comprehensive-integration maturity than technology infrastructure and top-level strategic commitment
readiness_statement: At a benchmark central enterprise independently recognized as a first-mover and industry leader in digital transformation (rated overall "digital pioneer" level, 3.24/5), only Infrastructure scored "Excellent" and Top-level Design, Business Process, and Digital Performance scored "Good," while Professional Management (organizational structure, financial management, HR management, R&D digitalization) and Comprehensive Integration both scored only "General" (mediocre) -- the two dimensions explicitly identified by the study as the key factors restricting further digital transformation.
mechanism: Technology infrastructure and top-level strategic commitment are comparatively easier to build and are highly visible to leadership and external benchmarking, so they mature first and fastest even in industry-leading firms; professional management (adapting organizational structure, HR, and financial processes to digital ways of working) and comprehensive integration (breaking down cross-departmental data silos) require deeper, less visible organizational change and therefore lag even when an enterprise is otherwise recognized as an industry digital leader.
operationalization_hint: When benchmarking digital-transformation readiness, do not infer that strong scores on infrastructure or leadership commitment imply strong organizational/integration maturity; explicitly assess professional-management and cross-departmental-integration dimensions separately, since these are the most likely residual bottleneck even in otherwise-mature organizations.
rationale: The case study classifies the enterprise as a digital pioneer but identifies professional management and comprehensive integration as general and as key restricting factors. The CF accurately captures this within-case maturity profile.

readiness_statement: At the case enterprise, horizontal integration (business-process integration with upstream/downstream partner enterprises across the value chain) scored "Excellent," while vertical integration (intra-enterprise integration between internal finance/business/R&D/production functions) scored only "General" -- despite both being sub-components of the single "Comprehensive Integration" dimension, they diverged sharply, with external, inter-organizational integration outpacing internal, cross-departmental integration.

spans.source_excerpt:
In this study, a total of 42 models are covered to better represent the changes in the digital maturity models over
time. However, the analysis also revealed the most common criteria in other words must-haves in the models such as
leadership, strategy, business model, customer focus, human capital etc. Safadi [32] conducted a similar analysis with
considering 20 digital maturity models and the study also revealed the same must-have criteria. In an earlier analysis
conducted by Safadi [33] 18 digital maturity model is examined, and results showed the importance of strategy,
organization, culture, technology, customer focus and human capital. Additionally, conducted literature review also
highlighted that the most common dimensions are listed as (i) culture, (ii) technology, (iii) operations & processes,
(iv) strategy, (v) organization, (vi) innovation, (vii) customer focus and (viii) leadership. In 2023, Aras and
Büyüközkan [34] examined the literature in detail and determined 6 basic dimensions such as (i) strategy, (ii) value,
(iii) processes, (iv) technology and data, (v) digital work and (vi) governance. From this point of view, the results that
are achieved inthis studyare considered as compatible withexistingliterature. However, since the analyses conducted
inthis studyfocus ona broader time interval and examine the latest models, the studyprovides beneficial data to guide
future studies bydeterminingcurrent model trends. Inother words, focusingona longer time period notonlyprovided,
a better understandingofhowbusinesses changed but also revealed howthey’ve started to thinkabout digital maturity.
By looking at these changes, this study contributes new insights to what is already known from other research.
Especially answering a new question “Which criteria are mentioned more in today's business environment?”, by
comparing time intervals, it is believed that this study directly contributed to future models.
It should be noted that the frequencies of the dimensions used vary depending on whether the models are sector-
based or not. In this respect, it is seen that different dimensions come to the fore in sector-oriented studies [35].
According to the sector of the company, digital technologycapabilities can be added including sub-criteria of big data,
cloud technologies, intelligent automation, artificial intelligence, robotics etc. [35] Moreover, managers can evaluate
their digital ecosystem including external users, resources and value chains. In this sense, type of the company will
affect the usage of criteria set such as agility management, digital marketing, assets management etc. Analysis show
that, more recently Cybersecurity, Energy management, Monitoring /Control, Digital Training, Fiscal management,
Digital policy and standards, Development lifecycle, Agility, Collaboration, and Validation gaining more importance.
However, usage of these dimensions should be carefully added to the maturity model. Although this study highlights
the changing structure of the models, this change should be evaluated by managers in terms of organizations’ own
capabilities.

readiness_statement: Digital governance (policies, structures, processes, and mechanisms establishing accountability and prioritization for digital initiatives) and digital leadership (vision, culture, and mindset that inspires innovation, collaboration, and agility) are conceptually distinct enablers of digital maturity, not a single "leadership" construct; without governance, DT efforts lack direction and compatibility with business objectives even if leaders are personally inspiring, while without inspiring leadership, governance structures alone fail to motivate genuine employee participation.

operationalization_hint: Assess digital governance (formal policies/accountability for digital initiatives) and digital leadership (vision-communication and culture-building capacity) as two separate readiness dimensions rather than folding them into one "leadership" item.

cluster_label: Dedicated digital leadership roles with real authority

4.1.1. Digital Governance and Leadership
Digital governance is a system for guiding digital transformation in electronic sports
businesses that establishes policies, structures, processes, and mechanisms to ensure the
acquisition of digital value and benefit. According to interviewee number 8, who is an
employee of an electronic sports business with 15 years of work experience, “digital
governance pursues two main objectives: first, coordination for prioritizing, synchronizing,
and aligning digital initiatives across the organization; second, sharing efficient resources to
achieve digital transformation goals”. Additionally, “digital leaders” are leaders who define
and frame digital age issues well, offer technology-based solutions for them, and coordinate
the elements of their organization to move towards digital transformation. In this regard,
interviewee number 4 stated, “Digital leaders know that the digital transformation story is
not just a technology story, but they consider strategy, culture, innovation, and employee
skills as circles alongside technology that are essential to guide the organization on the path
to digital transformation. Perhaps the most important role of digital leaders is to attract
enthusiastic employee participation in the path of digital transformation”.

readiness_statement: Organizations progressing toward digital maturity fall into distinct failure/success archetypes depending on whether they are strong in technological capability, leadership/governance capability, both, or neither: "digital enthusiasts" over-invest in every new digital tool but lack governance/coordination and therefore waste resources on non-adaptive, uncoordinated systems; "digital conservatives" have strong governance/leadership discipline but excessive caution prevents them from building powerful technological capabilities; only "digital leaders" excel at both and achieve superior results.
mechanism: Because technology adoption and leadership/governance capability can develop independently of each other, assessing only one (e.g., counting adopted technologies) misses organizations that are technologically active but organizationally incoherent, or vice versa; the two-axis typology exposes which specific combination of strengths and gaps an organization has.
operationalization_hint: When benchmarking an organization's digital maturity, plot it on both a technology-capability axis and a leadership/governance-capability axis rather than a single composite score, to correctly diagnose whether the binding constraint is technological or organizational.
rationale: The maturity typology explicitly distinguishes beginners, enthusiasts, conservatives, and leaders through contrasting technology and leadership/governance capability profiles.

raw_condition_label: digital-divide-aware maturity assessment incorporating infrastructure/skills/socioeconomic-cultural stages specific to developing-country context
readiness_statement: Digital transformation maturity assessment models developed for developed-country contexts are not directly transferable to developing countries because measurable maturity there must also account for a distinct "digital divide" progression (infrastructure access, skills, and outcomes) shaped by socioeconomic and cultural inequality factors (income, education, welfare, culture) not present as binding constraints in developed-economy models.
mechanism: Standard maturity dimensions (organization, technology, strategy, employees, customers, processes, culture) implicitly assume a baseline of infrastructure access and digital literacy that cannot be assumed in developing-country contexts, so an additional digital-divide-stage assessment is needed to correctly locate an organization's actual starting point.
operationalization_hint: When building or selecting a maturity assessment for a developing-country organization, add explicit digital-divide-stage items (infrastructure access, skills, outcomes) alongside the standard dimensions.
rationale: The maturity-model study explicitly frames the digital divide and developing-country context as relevant to maturity assessment, including infrastructure, skills, and socioeconomic context. The CF appropriately records a transferability boundary and an added assessment requirement for this context.

raw_condition_label: balance between digital capability (technological foundation) and digital impact (managerial/cultural leverage) factors is required for high digital maturity, not strength in either dimension alone
readiness_statement: Across a pilot test of 5 service-provider companies, the highest overall digital maturity was achieved only when both Digital Capability factors (strategy, competence, customer experience, technology) and Digital Impact factors (business model, smart services, leadership, culture) scored comparably high; companies strong on one dimension but weak on the other did not achieve higher overall maturity, confirming the model's key design principle that capability without impact-leverage (or vice versa) caps maturity.
mechanism: Digital Capability factors build the technological/organisational foundation, while Digital Impact factors determine whether that foundation is actually leveraged to respond to market/customer demand through new products, services, and business models; a strong foundation without leverage capability produces unused potential, and strong leverage capability without a foundation has nothing to leverage.
operationalization_hint: When assessing digital maturity, always score both a capability/foundation dimension and an impact/leverage dimension separately, and prioritize the weaker of the two rather than further strengthening whichever dimension is already strong.
page_or_section: Section 3.3 (Digital Service Transformation Maturity Matrix), Section 5.3
rationale: The maturity model defines Digital Capability as the digital foundation and Digital Impact as its organizational leverage, explicitly requires balance for high maturity, and directs action to the weaker dimension. The five-company pilot confirms practical use of the assessment logic. The CF is an accurate operationalization of the model's stated design principle.

raw_condition_label: digital competence/talent and customer-experience management consistently lag behind digital strategy maturity across service provider companies, even when strategy is well-developed
readiness_statement: In the pilot test of 5 service-provider companies, the "Digital Strategy" factor consistently scored highest among Digital Capability factors, while "Digital Competence" (digital skills, talent, HR-development for digitalization) and "Customer Experience" (simplification of interactions, management of expectations) consistently scored lowest -- indicating these companies feel confident about their digital strategy but lack the competence and customer-experience execution capability to actually deliver on it.
mechanism: A well-articulated digital strategy creates an expectation of execution capability that the organisation's actual digital skills base and customer-facing execution ability do not yet support, so strategy maturity running ahead of competence/execution maturity is a structural mismatch rather than a random variation, likely because strategy formulation requires fewer organisation-wide behavioral changes than building deep talent pipelines or redesigning customer interactions.
operationalization_hint: When a service organisation reports strong digital-strategy maturity, specifically audit digital-competence/talent and customer-experience execution capability before assuming the strategy will translate into results, since these are the most likely bottlenecks.
rationale: The pilot results explicitly report Digital Strategy subfactors as highest and Digital Competence and Customer Experience subfactors as lowest, with the stated interpretation.

mechanism: Culture-related capabilities (agility, collaboration, data-driven decision-making, leadership digital savvy) require sustained behavioral and mindset change across the whole organisation, which is inherently slower to develop than technology deployment or strategy formulation, explaining why culture consistently lags even in companies that have made real progress on more concrete, individually-actionable dimensions.
operationalization_hint: Treat digital-culture subfactors (innovation, agility, data-driven decisions, collaboration, leadership digital savvy) as long-lead-time investments requiring sustained multi-year effort, and do not expect them to improve at the same pace as technology or strategy-dimension scores.
rationale: The pilot interpretation identifies low maturity across most Digital Culture subfactors and a low ranking for leadership digital savvy, supporting the stated culture-related finding within the sampled service providers.

raw_condition_label: single-assessor digital maturity self-assessment risks systematic optimism bias from higher-hierarchy respondents; interdisciplinary, multi-level assessor panels are needed for accurate maturity scoring
readiness_statement: Experts who pilot-tested the DSTM assessment model explicitly flagged that not all aspects of digital maturity can be accurately assessed by one person, and that employees at higher levels of hierarchy tend to assess digital maturity more optimistically than employees at lower levels, meaning a single-assessor or management-only assessment process risks systematically overstating actual digital maturity.
mechanism: Senior respondents may have more visibility into strategic intent and less exposure to day-to-day execution friction than lower-hierarchy employees, biasing their self-assessment upward relative to the on-the-ground reality that lower-level employees experience directly.
operationalization_hint: Require digital maturity self-assessments to be completed by an interdisciplinary panel spanning multiple hierarchical levels (not just senior management), and treat single-respondent or management-only assessment scores as likely optimistic upper bounds rather than accurate current-state measures.
rationale: The authors report assessors' limitation that one person cannot assess all aspects and recommend an interdisciplinary, multi-hierarchy assessment group because senior staff may assess maturity more optimistically.

raw_condition_label: digital business model and digital ecosystem development are the least-addressed dimensions across existing digital maturity models, biasing most instruments toward exploiting existing technology over exploring new business models
readiness_statement: A systematic review of 22 existing digital maturity models found that the aspect of developing new digital business models is hardly addressed in almost any of them, and this gap was confirmed empirically in the pilot test, where "Digital Service Business Model" subfactors (framework, ecosystem) scored among the lowest of all Digital Impact factors even in companies that scored well on "Service Engineering & Innovation".
mechanism: Because most existing maturity models were developed with a technology-exploitation lens (assessing how well an organisation deploys and integrates digital tools), they systematically under-instrument the exploration-oriented capability of designing genuinely new digital business models and ecosystems, so organisations relying on these models to guide their DT roadmap will underinvest in business-model innovation relative to technology deployment.
operationalization_hint: When selecting or building a digital maturity assessment, explicitly check whether it includes dedicated business-model and digital-ecosystem-design criteria, since most existing models (and organisations following them) systematically underweight this dimension relative to technology and process dimensions.
rationale: The review of 22 maturity models finds digital business models hardly addressed; the pilot further shows low maturity for the business-model framework and ecosystem subfactors.

4. Digital Maturity Measurement (DX-SAMM Digital Transformation – Self Assessment Maturity Model)
This study proposes the development of a digital maturity model that considers multidimensional involvement to
facilitate the monitoring of digital maturity in organizations. Based on the literature review and the Comparative
Analysis Technique described in the previous chapter, a distribution of seven dimensions and 21 sub-dimensions
supporting the success of digital transformation was obtained. These dimensions and subdimensions were
subsequently proposed for inclusion in the development of a digital maturity model, referred to as the Digital
Transformation – Self Assessment Model (DX-SAMM), in this research. This model is intended to measure digital
maturity in organizations in a general sense [4]. Table 2 presents a general explanation of the proposed dimensions
and their accompanying subdimensions. The maturity level used in this study was adopted from the maturity level of
SPICE. It is part of the ISO/IEC 3300XX family of standards and is widely used as a reference model for maturity. In
addition, SPICE has been widely adopted for maturity measurement in various domains such as organizational agility
measurement, automotive, governance, and cross-domains. The maturity levels ranged from 0 to 5. Level 0 is called
incomplete and describes theDX requirement to be low. Level 1: Performed, indicating that the DX process had begun
Level 2: Managed DX processes are well-managed. Level 3: Established Process, The Digital transition process has
been carried out consistently in accordance with established standards. Level 4: Predictable and DX process
quantitative techniques are applied. Level 5: Optimizing, DX process evaluation is carried out[4][9][27][28][29].

Case studies evaluating the use of DX-SAMM were conducted in financial sector organizations with more than 200
employees and several branches. To ensure the accuracy of the results, organizations that had undertaken digital
transformation were selected. A management group session was formed to assist in the completion of the assessment.
Furthermore, the system processes the input results according to the answers to each question on a Likert scale. In
figure 2 (fig.2) the maturity levels of the seven dimensions are visualized.

6. Conclusion
In this study, a digital maturity measurement model called DX SAMM was developed. It is intended for monitoring
digital maturity measurements in general to be utilized by organizations in assessing their digital maturity
independently. This monitoring involves organizational management. The model in this research was developed using
several approaches, including a literature review, comparative analysis, design in the development of measurement
tools, and empirical validation with case studies. In this study, SPICE was adopted as a reference for maturity levels
in various domains. Unlike other digital maturity models, DX-SAMM emphasizes digital maturity measurements that

raw_condition_label: top-down technology-replication vs. bottom-up process-diagnostic approaches to structuring a digital transformation program, with explicit complementary trade-offs
readiness_statement: A digital transformation program can be structured either top-down (replicating already-proven pilot digital tools across similar processes, starting fast but risking missed problems due to insufficient diagnostic depth) or bottom-up (exhaustively diagnosing all business processes first to identify true pain points, more thorough but significantly delaying the start of transformation); the two approaches are not mutually exclusive and can be run in parallel if kept synchronized.
mechanism: The replication approach treats existing validated tools as the starting point (technology-first), while the process approach treats identified business problems as the starting point (problem-first); each approach's weakness is the other's strength, so combining them lets an organisation start delivering quick wins from replication while a parallel diagnostic effort surfaces problems replication alone would miss.
operationalization_hint: When designing a DT program roadmap, explicitly decide whether to lead with proven-tool replication (for speed) or full process diagnostics (for thoroughness), or run both in a deliberately synchronized parallel track rather than defaulting to only one.
rationale: The paper explicitly contrasts a top-down replication approach with a bottom-up diagnostic approach, identifies their respective limitations, and states that synchronized parallel use is possible.

readiness_statement: Managers' digital structure readiness (DRR) -- their preparedness and willingness to establish cross-functional teams, support the creation of digital leadership roles, and cultivate risk-tolerant structures -- positively and significantly predicts managers' intention to implement DT (beta=0.269, p<0.01), validated via PLS-SEM on 150 Chinese managers across 11 industries.
mechanism: Managers instrumental in shaping organizational culture, resource alignment, and strategic initiatives translate their personal readiness to build supportive structures directly into a stronger intention to act on DT, because structural readiness defines the conditions under which DT-supporting behaviors become organizationally possible.
operationalization_hint: Assess individual managers' willingness to design cross-functional teams, support CDO-type roles, and tolerate risk-taking as a distinct readiness indicator, separate from their technology attitudes or strategic knowledge.
rationale: The paper defines managerial digital structure readiness as willingness to establish cross-functional teams, supportive structures, CDO roles, and risk-taking cultures, and its PLS-SEM result supports H1 with beta 0.269 and p below 0.01. rationale: The results report a positive, statistically significant DTR-to-implementation-intention association (beta 0.231, p<0.05) and show it is smaller than the other two readiness paths.

operationalization_hint: When selecting or developing managers to lead DT initiatives, prioritize assessing and building their strategic-alignment competence (ability to formulate goals, allocate resources, link digital initiatives to business strategy) over generic technology enthusiasm, since this was the strongest validated predictor of implementation intention.
rationale: The results report digital strategy readiness as the largest of the three estimated readiness paths to managers' intention to implement DT (beta 0.346, p<0.001).

raw_condition_label: government-specific digital maturity assessment requires adapting private-sector consulting models into a tailored, literature- and practitioner-validated framework rather than applying commercial models directly
readiness_statement: Conventional digital maturity assessment frameworks, mainly constructed by consulting firms for private/commercial organizations, are often unsuitable for government bodies due to fundamental differences in operational mission (value-oriented rather than profit-oriented) and structure; this study built a government-tailored 8-category, 34-factor framework by combining three consulting-firm models, academic literature validation (confirming 25 of 34 factors), and an 88-expert practitioner survey (Cronbach's alpha 0.955) across six GCC countries.
mechanism: Private-sector maturity models are optimized for profit-driven objectives and market competition, while government digital transformation is motivated by service delivery, transparency, and constrained-resource stewardship; applying an unmodified private-sector model risks measuring the wrong success criteria and missing government-specific factors, which only a purpose-built, cross-validated framework can address.
operationalization_hint: Do not apply commercial/consulting-firm digital maturity models unmodified to public-sector organizations; instead, adapt them through literature validation and practitioner consultation specific to the public-sector mission and operating context before use.
rationale: The paper states that consulting-firm maturity frameworks often fail in public-sector application, then describes a government-specific framework developed from consulting models, literature input, and an 88-expert cross-country survey with strong internal consistency.

mechanism: Leadership and management roles are positioned to receive and communicate top-down strategic direction (e.g., direct instructions from a minister), giving them a more favorable view of strategy execution, while technical experts working directly with infrastructure daily encounter its limitations first-hand, producing a systematically more critical assessment than leadership's more removed, strategic vantage point.
operationalization_hint: When surveying digital transformation maturity, disaggregate results by respondent role (leadership vs. technical/operational) rather than averaging across roles, since role-based perception gaps on strategy and infrastructure specifically can mask where real problems lie.
rationale: The role analysis reports significant job-title differences for Strategy and Vision, lower ratings by academic/consulting roles, and more critical infrastructure ratings by technical experts, while age, education, and experience were nonsignificant.

raw_condition_label: three-layered socio-technical structure (organizational readiness outer layer, agile delivery middle layer, project artefacts inner layer) as an operationalization of CSF interdependency for agile DT governance
readiness_statement: The 14 validated CSFs map onto three interdependent layers -- an outer Organizational Readiness layer (management commitment, team capability, organizational environment) that conditions an inner Agile Delivery layer (project management process, customer involvement, project manager capability, team environment, digital solution delivery strategy, project definition process, technological adaptability), which in turn conditions an innermost Project Artefacts layer (project nature, type, cost, schedule) -- reflecting how outer structural enablers determine the effectiveness of inner technical and procedural processes.
mechanism: Grounded in socio-technical systems theory, the layered structure formalizes that technology and project-management tools (inner layers) only deliver value when embedded within a supportive social/organizational system (outer layer); attempting to strengthen inner-layer factors without first securing outer-layer readiness will not produce proportional improvements in DT outcomes.
operationalization_hint: When diagnosing why an agile-DT initiative is underperforming despite strong technical execution, check the outer Organizational Readiness layer first (leadership commitment, culture, team capability) before troubleshooting the middle Agile Delivery or inner Project Artefact layers.
rationale: The study maps 14 validated subfactors to organizational readiness, agile delivery, and project artefacts and explicitly interprets outer structural enablers as conditioning inner technical processes.

spans.source_excerpt:
Our study advances this discourse by integrating diverse success factors from across
17 empirical and conceptual studies and validating them through a structured Delphi-
AHP approach. This process yielded a hierarchy of 14 sub-factors that map onto three
interrelated layers—organizational readiness, agile delivery, and project artefacts, as shown
in Figure 2. This layered framework offers a novel contribution by aligning the empirical
findings with the core logic of STS theory, revealing how the outer structural enablers
condition the effectiveness of the inner technical processes.
Figure 2. Layered structure of critical success factors in agile-based digital transformation projects.

The outermost layer of our proposed framework—Organizational Readiness—
represents the foundational enablers of agile-based digital transformation (DT). This layer
encompasses key factors such as management commitment, team capability, and the
broader organizational environment. These dimensions reflect an organization’s strategic
alignment, cultural adaptability, and institutional capacity to support agile practices at
scale. Guided by socio-technical systems (STS) theory—which emphasizes the joint opti-
mization of technical and social subsystems for sustainable transformation [83,84]—this
layer constitutes the critical social infrastructure that allows agile methodologies to be
effectively embedded and sustained. Agile tools and processes alone are insufficient when
implemented within rigid hierarchies or misaligned governance structures.

raw_condition_label: technology maturity (TRL) and organizational digital maturity (Acatech MI) are statistically independent dimensions, both jointly necessary for successful digital transformation planning
readiness_statement: Text-mining analysis (cosine similarity of keyword-occurrence vectors, validated by a 1000-iteration permutation test yielding an empirical p-value of 0.000) shows that the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) scale and the Acatech Industry 4.0 Maturity Index (MI) are near-orthogonal (~86-87 degree angle between vectors), confirming that technology maturity and organizational digital maturity are conceptually and statistically independent constructs that must both be assessed, since a highly mature technology can fail in a low-maturity organization and vice versa.
mechanism: Because the two frameworks were developed independently for different purposes (TRL for technology risk assessment originating at NASA; MI for organizational digital-transformation staging), their near-orthogonality is not coincidental but reflects that they measure genuinely separate readiness constructs -- technology push versus organization pull -- neither of which can substitute for the other.
operationalization_hint: When planning any technology-integration or R&D initiative, score both the technology's TRL and the organization's Acatech MI level separately rather than assuming a high score on one implies readiness on the other.
page_or_section: Section 3 (Method), text-mining analysis and permutation test
rationale: The authors empirically show near-perpendicular text-mining vectors for the technology-roadmap and Acatech maturity concepts and report a 1,000-iteration permutation test with empirical p=.000, supporting their interpretation of distinct readiness dimensions.

spans.source_excerpt:
Since we are going to measure two different indicators, a reflection on their indepen-
dence and/or orthogonality is necessary. The two readiness dimensions, the Industry 4.0
level and technology level, are theoretically independent since they assess the readiness of
the company with respect to the Industry 4.0 paradigm and the readiness of the specific
technology to be applied in the specific context. To check the orthogonality of the two
dimensions, we perform a comparative analysis based on text mining.
We apply a Natural Language Processing algorithm on textual descriptions from the
Wikipedia page on a technology roadmap (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_
roadmap, accessed on 25 May 2025) and the section of the official Acatech study [44]
describing the maturity levels. To discern the similarities and differences between the
two texts, we extract keywords by tokenizing the content, eliminating stop words and
numbers, and retaining words with occurrences equal to or greater than 4—a threshold
considered relevant for both texts. The resulting normalized vectors of word occurrences,
shown in Appendix A, were then subjected to a cosine similarity analysis. Computing the
scalar product of the two normalized vectors yielded a value of 0.077 that corresponds to an
arccosine of 85.55 degrees, which shows how the two-unit vectors are almost perpendicular.
The angle of about 90 degrees indicates that the two vectors of keywords’ occurrences are
orthogonal and thus suggests that the two domains are almost independent. This quantita-
tive approach sheds light on the distinct thematic focuses of the technology roadmap and
the Industrie 4.0 Maturity Index. Almost the same can be said when comparing, following

--- PAGE 10 ---
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 7172 10 of 27
the same method, the original description of TRLs by [32] to the Acatech study. Appendix B
shows the normalized vectors of word occurrences, and the resulting scalar product is 0.048
that corresponds to an arccosine of 87.27 degrees. Also, in this case, the two vectors are
almost perpendicular, and thus, the two domains are almost orthogonal (i.e., independent).
This demonstrates that not only is the TRM orthogonal to the digital domain, but also that
the TRL measures aspects that differ from what Acatech does. To evaluate whether this low
similarity could have occurred by chance, we conducted a non-parametric permutation
test with 1000 iterations. In each iteration, the combined token pool from both documents
was randomly shuffled and split into two new pseudo-documents preserving the original
token counts of the TRM and Acatech texts. For each pair, we constructed term–frequency
vectors using the same fixed vocabulary, applied normalization, and computed the cosine
similarity. Across all 1000 permutations, none produced a similarity rate as low as the
observed value of 0.048, resulting in an empirical p-value of 0.000. This strongly indicates
that the similarity between the original texts is significantly lower than what would be
expected by chance. Hence, the result statistically corroborates the interpretation that the
TRM and Acatech documents are thematically independent, providing robust support for
their conceptual orthogonality. Therefore, the two perspectives based on the 6 levels of
Acatech study and on the 9 TRLs could help to properly map digitalization and innovation
projects, taking into account the two distinct but interconnected perspectives.

mechanism: People react to change with both cognitive and emotional responses; when a Change Agent listens to and reflects a stakeholder's FOR back to them without judgment, the stakeholder feels understood and shifts from defending a position to exploring their own thoughts and motives, which reduces resistance more effectively than presenting additional facts or logical arguments.
operationalization_hint: Before or alongside standard requirements-gathering and sprint-planning activities, have a designated change agent map each stakeholder group's frame of reference (concerns, incentives, prior experience with similar changes) and tailor communication content and channel to that frame rather than using one uniform message.

rationale: The framework contrasts the cognitive focus of PMBOK and Scrum with emotional responses to uncertainty and prescribes communication from stakeholders' Frame of Reference without judgment.

readiness_statement: Across three case organizations (factory automation, local government, utility services), EA information consistently refines from coarse-grained strategic content (vision, drivers, desired results produced by the sensing capability) to tactical content (solution ideas, portfolios, gap analyses produced by the mobilizing capability) to fine-grained operational content (directives and guidelines that enable the transforming capability to actually reconfigure resources) -- with explicit feedback loops connecting all three levels back to strategy.
mechanism: Because sensing, mobilizing, and transforming are sequentially dependent dynamic sub-capabilities, the EA information each produces must progressively increase in granularity and specificity to be usable by the next capability; a strategic-level input (e.g., a vision statement) cannot directly drive operational transformation without being refined through the intermediate mobilizing stage into concrete solution ideas and resource-mobilization plans.
operationalization_hint: When designing EA governance for digital transformation, explicitly design the information hand-off from strategic (sensing) to tactical (mobilizing) to operational (transforming) artifacts as a deliberate refinement pipeline with feedback loops, rather than assuming strategic documents alone will inform operational execution.

raw_condition_label: organizational core values act as an implicit interpretive filter connecting vision to digital transformation decisions, though vision documents themselves risk being perceived as non-functional "window dressing"
readiness_statement: In two of three case organizations, core cultural values (e.g., a local government's stated commitment to "openness and transparency") were found to actively shape how vision-derived desired results were elaborated and pursued, demonstrating that values function as a live interpretive filter on strategic sensing -- yet in the same organization, the CIO explicitly questioned whether the published vision was authentic guidance or "just meant as window dressing to make us look better," while a factory-automation strategy manager treated the mission/vision as a genuine and consistently invoked starting point for all change initiatives.
mechanism: Vision statements only function as effective sensing-capability inputs when stakeholders perceive them as authentic and operative rather than as marketing artifacts; core values appear to be a more consistently trusted and operative guide across organizations than formally documented vision statements, suggesting values may be a more reliable EA-information input than vision documents in organizations where vision credibility is in question.
operationalization_hint: When using EA vision/mission artifacts to drive digital transformation sensing, first verify (e.g., via stakeholder interviews) whether the vision is perceived internally as authentic strategic guidance or as symbolic messaging, and supplement or substitute it with documented core organizational values where vision credibility is low.
page_or_section: Section IV.A (EA information driving the sensing capability)
rationale: The cases show core values shaping vision-derived desired results and contrast a questioned, marketing-like vision with a mission/vision treated as a starting point for change initiatives.

mechanism: If organizations tend to invest in visible technology infrastructure first because it is the most immediately actionable lever, while strategic and ecosystem capabilities require organizational maturity and experience gained from the earlier technology/organizational-change phases before they can be meaningfully developed, this would explain a natural (rather than merely coincidental) sequencing pattern.

raw_condition_label: seven foundational capability building blocks recur across the full breadth of IT capability domains and provide a tractable focus for capability improvement programs
readiness_statement: A concept-centric analysis of all 36 IT capabilities and 315 sub-elements (Capability Building Blocks) in the IT Capability Maturity Framework (IT-CMF) identified seven recurring Foundational Capability Building Blocks -- Governance, Resourcing, Roles/Responsibilities/Accountabilities, Skills and Competence Development, Culture, Stakeholder Management, and Communication -- that appear across the large majority of the 36 distinct IT capability domains.
mechanism: Because these seven elements recur so consistently across otherwise-distinct capability domains (from risk management to enterprise architecture to innovation management), maturing them has a multiplying effect across the entire IT capability portfolio, letting organizations focus a capability-improvement program on a manageable number of generically-applicable areas instead of independently maturing all 36 domain-specific capabilities.
operationalization_hint: When planning an IT/digital capability improvement program, prioritize maturing the seven foundational building blocks (governance, resourcing, roles/accountabilities, skills, culture, stakeholder management, communication) as cross-cutting investments rather than treating each of the 36+ specific IT capability domains as requiring independent improvement effort.
rationale: The concept-centric analysis identifies seven higher-order recurring building-block categories across the majority of IT-CMF capabilities and frames them as a manageable basis for capability improvement.

operationalization_hint: When resourcing digital transformation initiatives, adopt pay-for-use or service-based cost models for digital platforms and services rather than fixed annual budget allocations, while maintaining traditional budgeting for the stable operational backbone.
rationale: The literature-based discussion states that traditional funding models do not effectively support digital service delivery and identifies a shift toward dynamic pay-for-use or service-based cost models.

readiness_statement: Beyond establishing a formal communication plan and channels, effectively managing bi-directional information exchange (listening and responding to stakeholder feedback) demonstrates respect and increases trust, while informal conversations between digital-transformation leaders and other stakeholders promote collegiality, bonding, rapport, and a shared understanding of the project vision.
mechanism: A one-way, top-down communication plan (however well-designed) only transmits information; it is the act of listening and visibly responding to feedback, plus informal relationship-building outside formal channels, that signals respect and builds the trust needed for stakeholders to remain committed through a long transformation process.

rationale: The paper explicitly calls for managed bi-directional exchange, listening and responding to feedback, and informal conversations as mechanisms for respect, trust, collegiality, and shared understanding.

readiness_statement: Across 33 interviews spanning multiple industries and hierarchy levels, the decision to structurally separate versus integrate a digital initiative is best driven by two joint criteria: (1) whether the activity is exploratory (radical, future-oriented, high-risk) or exploitative (incremental, efficiency-focused, using existing products/processes) and (2) how close the activity is to the core business; distant exploration should be separated (e.g., in an innovation hub, think tank, or spun-off unit), while exploitation close to the core should be integrated, with exploration close to the core admitting either option depending on additional risk factors.
mechanism: Distant exploration needs freedom, dedicated budget, and different processes/culture that a core organization's follow-up-oriented, efficiency-focused culture would suppress, whereas exploitation requires deep process/product/customer knowledge that only exists within the core organization, so applying the wrong structural choice in either direction either stifles innovation or produces solutions disconnected from real business needs.
operationalization_hint: Before deciding whether to structurally separate a digital initiative, explicitly classify it on two axes -- exploration vs. exploitation, and closeness to the core business -- and use the resulting quadrant (not intuition or a blanket "digital vs. non-digital" split) to decide on separation, integration, or a hybrid approach with safeguards.
rationale: The 33-interview study states that separation/integration depends on exploration or exploitation and closeness to the core, recommending separation for distant exploration and integration for core-connected exploitation.

rationale: The findings identify favoritism and perceived injustice risks from digital/core separation and state that weak links prevent digital knowledge and mindsets transferring to the core business.

raw_condition_label: digital maturity grade functions as a temporal trigger for re-evaluating separation/integration decisions: early-stage transformation favors separation to build digital literacy, while increasing maturity favors integration
readiness_statement: The digital maturity grade of an incumbent company acts as a trigger point for rethinking organizational separation decisions: early in a digital transformation, separating digital activities helps generate a startup culture and build digital literacy that does not yet exist internally, but as the company matures and grows closer to the core business, the pull for digital improvements in the core business increases, becoming a trigger to dissolve or integrate the previously separate digital hub.
mechanism: Early separation solves a bootstrapping problem (lack of internal digital knowledge/culture), but that same separation becomes counterproductive once digital capability has matured, because continued separation at that stage blocks exactly the core-business integration and efficiency gains the company set out to capture -- meaning the optimal organizational structure is not fixed but should be re-evaluated as maturity increases.
operationalization_hint: Treat organizational separation/integration decisions as time-bound, not permanent: schedule periodic re-assessment of digital maturity grade specifically as a trigger to revisit whether a previously separated digital unit should now be integrated into the core business.
rationale: The results identify digital maturity grade as a trigger to reconsider separation: early separation builds literacy and startup culture, whereas greater maturity and core-business pull trigger hub dissolution/integration.

mechanism: Full-time separation loses core-business knowledge transfer, while full integration loses the freedom/speed benefits of a dedicated exploration space; a flexible, limited-time rotation structure captures both benefits simultaneously by having the same individuals carry knowledge across the boundary rather than requiring the organizational boundary itself to dissolve.
operationalization_hint: When structural separation is chosen for digital exploration, add a temporal-ambidexterity mechanism (e.g., scheduled rotations, one-day-a-week arrangements) so that core-business employees gain exposure to the innovation hub and hub employees stay connected to core-business needs, rather than leaving the two groups permanently isolated from one another.
rationale: The study gives the one-day-per-week example and explicitly explains temporal ambidexterity as mutual transfer of process/product knowledge and digital skills across a hub/core boundary.

authors: Breitruck, M.
raw_condition_label: digital maturity models fail to deliver transformation value primarily due to systemic organizational barriers -- stakeholder inclusion, strategic-goal misalignment, governance anchoring, and workflow/iteration integration -- not merely model-design flaws
readiness_statement: Applying a socio-technical-systems lens (People, Structure, Task, Technology) to why Digital Maturity Models fail to support digital transformation steering, an exploratory interview study found that issues extend well beyond the DMM's own design (complexity, inflexibility, context-fit): missing stakeholder inclusion beyond the steering committee, absent leadership involvement, lack of strategic-goal linkage, insufficient governance anchoring of DMM outputs into the transformation process, and inadequate workflow/iteration integration all independently degrade or eliminate DMM value, even when the model itself is well-designed.
mechanism: A DMM is a socio-technical artifact whose value depends on the surrounding organizational system (people, structure, task processes), not just the technical artifact itself, so organizations that select or build a well-designed DMM but neglect stakeholder engagement, governance anchoring, or iterative re-application will still see the model abandoned or underutilized regardless of its technical quality.
operationalization_hint: When adopting any digital maturity model as an operationalization/assessment tool, budget explicit attention (beyond model selection or design) to stakeholder inclusion across all affected groups, leadership visible buy-in, governance structures for translating DMM outputs into transformation actions, and a defined iteration/update cadence -- treating these as prerequisites for value, not optional extras.
rationale: The exploratory findings identify stakeholder inclusion and leadership involvement, then describe strategic alignment, governance structuring, workflow integration, and iteration as barriers to deriving DMM value.

raw_condition_label: maturity-model-prescribed capabilities can structurally conflict with an organization's strategy-first goal-setting approach, since DMMs typically reverse the sequence by prescribing capabilities toward a predefined target state
readiness_statement: Organizations typically approach strategic topics by first defining their strategy and then identifying the capabilities needed to achieve it, but DMMs frequently reverse this sequence by prescribing the capabilities required to meet a predefined (often peer-group-derived) target maturity state that the organization cannot easily adjust -- creating a structural mismatch between the organization's own strategy-formulation logic and the DMM's built-in logic that was identified as a specific barrier to DMM adoption.
mechanism: Because DMMs are usually built from generic industry best-practice or peer-group benchmarks rather than an individual organization's specific strategic goals, applying a DMM's prescribed capability targets can feel like being handed someone else's destination rather than a tool for reaching one's own, undermining buy-in and usage even when the model's content is otherwise sound.
operationalization_hint: Before applying a DMM as a steering tool, explicitly reconcile its prescribed target-state capabilities with the organization's own strategy-first goal-setting process, and be prepared to adapt or reinterpret DMM benchmarks rather than treating them as a substitute for organization-specific goal derivation.
page_or_section: Section 4 (Structure component: strategic alignment and governance)
rationale: The study describes a strategic-alignment mismatch where organizations work strategy-to-capability while DMMs can prescribe fixed target capabilities; this is documented as a Structure-component barrier.

paper_authors: Park, H.U.; Kim, S.K.; Lee, D.H.; Rho, J.J.
authors: Park, H.U.; Kim, S.K.; Lee, D.H.; Rho, J.J.
raw_condition_label: digital transformation readiness should be modeled as a non-compensatory distribution of strategic attention across interdependent domains, not as an additive composite of domain capability levels
readiness_statement: A two-round Delphi study (53 experts, Kendall's W=0.51) demonstrates that digital transformation readiness is better captured as a configurational pattern of how strategic attention is allocated across seven interdependent domains (Competition, Customer, Data, Innovation, Regulation, Technology, Value) than as an additive/compensatory composite score, because in interdependent systems underdevelopment in one domain constrains the effectiveness of investments in others -- meaning strength in one domain cannot substitute for weakness in another, contrary to the compensatory logic implicit in most maturity models and composite readiness indices.
mechanism: Additive/compensatory scoring assumes domains are independent contributors to an overall score, but complementarity theory shows that the marginal return on investment in one domain depends on the development level of related domains, so an organization can appear "digitally mature" in aggregate while having a critical, unaddressed imbalance that a compensatory score would mask entirely.
operationalization_hint: When designing or interpreting any digital transformation readiness/maturity assessment, avoid producing a single aggregated score; instead, report and interpret domain-level scores as a distribution/profile, explicitly flagging domains that are low relative to their structural importance rather than allowing high scores elsewhere to offset them.
rationale: The SFI explicitly adopts a non-compensatory domain-profile logic, stating that under-emphasis in one structurally interdependent domain cannot be offset by strength in others; the Delphi reports W approximately .51.

raw_condition_label: customer engagement and value-creation domains consistently receive the highest strategic-attention weight among seven digital-transformation domains, while regulation and competition consistently receive the lowest
readiness_statement: Across a 53-expert Delphi panel, Customer (26.99% weight) and Value (22.43% weight) domains together account for nearly half of total strategic-attention weight in digital transformation, followed by Data (13.98%) and Innovation (13.91%), with Technology (11.08%) forming a secondary layer, while Regulation (6.42%) and Competition (5.20%) receive the lowest weights -- a stable pattern confirmed across two Delphi rounds with minimal variation (average rank change ~0.05).
mechanism: Experts consistently prioritize domains with direct, near-term value-creation impact (customer engagement, business-model value capture) over domains addressing external constraints (regulation) or positioning (competition), likely because the former are more directly actionable and within organizational control, while the latter are perceived as boundary conditions rather than primary transformation levers.
operationalization_hint: When prioritizing digital transformation investment under resource constraints, expect and validate that customer-engagement and value-creation initiatives will typically be favored over regulatory-compliance or competitive-positioning initiatives, and treat significant deviation from this pattern (e.g., disproportionate regulation focus) as worth investigating for context-specific justification.
rationale: The final SFI configuration reports Customer 26.99% and Value 22.43% as the two largest weights and Regulation 6.42% and Competition 5.20% as the smallest.

mechanism: Because domains are interdependent, a domain's low relative priority reflects its role as an enabling/constraining boundary condition rather than a primary value-creation lever; removing attention to it entirely (rather than proportionally reducing it) risks removing a necessary condition for the higher-priority domains to function, which a simple ranked-priority list could obscure.
operationalization_hint: When using any domain-prioritization framework to allocate digital transformation resources, retain a baseline minimum investment in low-weighted but structurally necessary domains (e.g., regulatory compliance, competitive monitoring) rather than deprioritizing them to zero, even when they rank last in strategic-attention weight.
rationale: The authors explicitly caution that Regulation and Competition's lower weights do not imply dispensability because they define boundary conditions whose underdevelopment can constrain overall coherence.

rationale: The diagnostic guidance expressly requires jointly considering gap magnitude and structural importance, noting that moderate gaps in high-importance domains can warrant earlier intervention.

raw_condition_label: organizational agility for digital transformation manifests as two structurally opposite but equally valid paths: liquid/project-based dissolution of departments versus stable hierarchy with new agility-specific roles layered in
readiness_statement: Across 16 expert interviews, organizational agility for digital transformation was described in two distinct, non-overlapping ways: (1) a "liquid organisation" path that dissolves classical departments and functions in favor of project-oriented, competency-based grouping with leaders acting as moderators rather than supervisors, and (2) a stable, hierarchical organisation that retains its classical organisational chart but layers in new agility-enabling roles (e.g., data scientist, community manager, digital consultant) to inject quick-response capability without restructuring.
mechanism: Both paths achieve the same underlying goal -- faster response to market opportunities and changing circumstances -- through different mechanisms: the liquid path removes structural friction by eliminating departmental boundaries entirely, while the role-injection path adds specialized quick-response capacity into an otherwise unchanged structure, meaning organizations do not have to choose between "agile" and "traditional" as a binary but can select the path matching their risk tolerance for restructuring.
operationalization_hint: When assessing or designing organizational agility for digital transformation, do not assume agility requires abandoning hierarchy; consider whether a targeted new-roles approach within the existing structure could achieve comparable responsiveness with lower disruption than a full liquid-organization redesign.
page_or_section: Section 5.2 (New structural requirements: Agility of organisational structure)
rationale: The interviews distinguish a liquid, project-oriented organization from a stable hierarchy augmented with new digital roles; both are presented as routes to quick responsiveness.

readiness_statement: Interviewees' understanding of "culture of change" as a digital-transformation structural requirement split into two distinct modes: a disruptive mode emphasizing radical rethinking and reorientation, abandoning old structures to find new ways of operating, and an evolutionary mode characterized simply by tolerating mistakes and treating them as improvement opportunities (e.g., accepting that "five projects fail") without any other fundamental changes.
mechanism: Treating "culture of change" as a single undifferentiated construct risks organizations pursuing failure-tolerance initiatives (the evolutionary mode) while believing they have achieved the deeper structural reorientation the disruptive mode requires, or vice versa attempting radical reorientation without first establishing the failure-tolerant conditions that make experimentation psychologically safe.
operationalization_hint: When assessing an organization's "culture of change" readiness, explicitly distinguish whether the goal is evolutionary failure-tolerance (a necessary but lower-intensity precondition) or disruptive structural reorientation (a more intensive, less common transformation), since these require different interventions and should not be conflated in a single culture-readiness score.

rationale: The interview evidence separates disruptive, fundamental change from an evolutionary culture of mistakes and experimentation, including the failure-tolerance example.
