In contrast, “communicates with” is a bi-directional (i.e. symmetric) dependency.
Dependency data for the BioPharma enterprise architecture was obtained using a combination
of manual and automated methods. In particular, interviews were conducted with the IT director
and surveys were conducted with IT Service Owners. This information was then supplemented
with the use of open-source and custom tools to monitor the server and network traffic in the
system. Data on processes and communication links was then manually aggregated to the level
of the individual component. Importantly, many links discovered using automatic tools had been
overlooked by or were unknown to the IT Service Owners. This indicates that the theoretical (i.e.
documented) system architecture can deviate substantially from the actual architecture “in use,”

For managers, our methodology provides a clear picture of the actual instantiated architecture
that they possess, as opposed to high level conceptual representations often found in documents
depicting a firm’s IT architecture. The insights thereby generated will prove useful in several
ways, including i) helping to plan the allocation of resources to different components, based
upon predictions of the relative ease/difficulty of change; ii) monitoring the evolution of an
architecture over time, as new components and/or dependencies are introduced (e.g. when a new
firm is acquired) and; iii) identifying opportunities to improve the architecture, for instance, by
reducing coupling, and hence reducing the cost to change specific components.
Ironically, in this era of “big data,” the lack of appropriately granular data may be the largest
barrier to the systematic investigation of an enterprise architecture using our methodology. At a
minimum, firms need to capture data on the dependencies between different components in the
enterprise architecture, and the way that these dependencies evolve over time. To fully use this
data, they must also systematically capture performance data on the cost of change for
components over time. In most organizations we have worked with, this type of data does not
exist. In some, efforts have been made to collect this data manually. However, there are many
challenges associated with this approach, including a lack of incentives to provide accurate and
timely information. In this study, we found substantial omissions in the data collected via survey,
in comparison to the automated tools we used to uncover system dependencies. In essence, many
firms do not know the “real” enterprise IT architecture that they possess. As Eppinger and

raw_condition_label: process mining as a quantitative validation mechanism for EA compliance/alignment assessment, replacing subjective architect judgment with data-driven evidence
readiness_statement: The organization complements its formalized EA model (ArchiMate business/application/technology layers) with business process mining applied to event logs from the actual IT systems in use (e.g., SAP S/4 HANA), so that EA compliance principles such as "a system is supporting and aligned with business processes and avoids functional redundancy" are assessed via quantitative deviation analysis of real operational data rather than the qualitative, subjective judgment of the architect or system owner alone.
mechanism: Prior EA maturity/compliance assessments (e.g., heat maps scoring "P/M/L/F" per principle) relied on the architect's or solution owner's subjective estimation; applying process mining to event logs reveals actual process variants and deviations (e.g., multiple undocumented variants of an engineering-change-request process), giving enterprise architects concrete, quantitative evidence to replace or supplement subjective compliance scores and to lead better-informed discussions with stakeholders.
operationalization_hint: For EA principles framed as compliance/alignment checks (e.g., "system X avoids functional redundancy with process Y"), set up a process-mining case against the system's event logs before finalizing a qualitative maturity score, prioritizing processes most critical to downstream data quality/traceability.
rationale: The PLM method uses event-log process mining to compare actual practice with formalized EA and replace a subjective alignment/compliance assessment with quantitative evidence.

raw_condition_label: continuous EA-monitoring cycle combining formal modeling with operational data feedback is needed to keep pace with dynamic, multidisciplinary PLM/engineering environments
readiness_statement: The organization treats EA modeling (formalizing business processes, applications, and infrastructure in one repository) and EA evaluation (via process mining and maturity scorecards) as a permanent, cyclical 8-step process -- design, evaluate, decide, design solution, validate conformance, implement, review, re-model -- rather than a one-time architecture documentation exercise, specifically because engineering/PLM domains combine a need for IT-architecture stability with a need for high flexibility in domain-specific authoring tools, which continuously threatens to drift the as-documented EA away from actual practice.
mechanism: Cross-functional, multidisciplinary engineering domains require variety and flexibility in domain-specific tools (CAx, design automation) that business units adopt for their own efficiency, without necessarily complying with company-wide EA standards, causing downstream data-quality issues; and the emergence of mixed on-premise/cloud PLM solutions further complicates governance -- so the EA model must be continuously revalidated against actual operational data (via process mining) rather than assumed accurate once documented.
operationalization_hint: In engineering/PLM contexts where business units frequently adopt their own domain-specific authoring tools, schedule recurring EA-model-vs-operational-data reconciliation cycles (steps 1-2 and 7-8 of the continuous improvement method) rather than a single upfront EA documentation effort.
rationale: The method specifies an eight-step continuous-improvement cycle from formal EA modeling through process-based evaluation, solution implementation and review, back to EA-model adaptation.

Business process mining is an established technology that has gained recent interest

business process mining in the context of the core applications of PLM such as the

3 EA Method for continuous improvement of PLM
As highlighted in the review of the state of the art, existing methods from the field of
enterprise architecture do not feature the continuous evolution process required to man-
age the dynamics of enterprise architecture within thefield ofPLM. Hence,in this work
we propose a method featuring both the agility and flexibility required to account for
the opportunities stemming from emerging technologies in the context of PLM as well
as the monitoring capabilities required to guarantee streamlined application of these
technologies based on process mining. The method is illustrated in Figure 1.

As can be seen in Figure 1, the method presented in this work is based on the main
principles of continuous improvement [40], [41] so that the dynamics of PLM can be
taken into account. The method is constituted by the following steps:
1. The enterprise architecture is formalized using the ArchiMate modelling lan-
guage. The business processes, related applications as well as the supporting
infrastructure are captured holistically in one model repository. Each architec-
ture artifact is then documented with additional metadata that will be used for
the EA assessment.
2. The enterprise architecture is evaluated based on a comparison of the formal-
ized EA with the practically applied PLM processes. The monitoring of pro-
cesses as well as the evaluation of multiple dimensions of PLM maturity [42],
[43] such as the level of IT alignment allow to draw a balanced scorecard in-
dicating the maturity of a selected process.
3. Based on the yielded score card, informed decisions regarding the adaptation
of the EA can be taken. Potential actions include the adaption of business pro-
cesses, the inclusion/exclusion of specific application functions etc.
4. A potential solution reflecting the changes within the EA to realize the previ-
ouslydefinedaction isdesignedbythesolutionarchitects.Definingapotential
solution follows basic software development principles as defined in ISO
25010 [44]
5. Thepotentialsolution isevaluatedwith respecttonon-functionalrequirements
reflecting the EA conformance.
6. When conformance is guaranteed, the solution is implemented and integrated
to the enterprise IT systems.
7. The newly integrated IT solution is reviewed with respect to functional re-
quirements and if necessary adapted.
8. The EA model is adapted to incorporate the newly integrated IT solutions.
Step 1 and step 8 encompass the same activity of EA modeling. Hence, these actions
indicated the continuous character of the method that should be permanently applied to
ensure robustness, flexibility and efficiency of modern engineering companies.

authors: Grave, F.; van de Wetering, R.; Kusters, R.
raw_condition_label: EA practice value depends on jointly managing EA practice assimilation, success factors, and inhibitors as three interacting factor groups
readiness_statement: The organization manages EA artifact-enabled value creation by jointly attending to three interacting factor groups: EA practice assimilation (the diversity, breadth, and depth of EA use across the organization), EA practice success factors (awareness/benefits acknowledgment, sufficient artifact quality/availability, architect knowledge/skill, correct organizational anchoring, and stakeholder commitment/engagement), and EA practice inhibitors -- rather than treating any one group (e.g., just "getting artifacts adopted") in isolation.
mechanism: Prior EA-value research has examined assimilation, success factors, and inhibitors as separate research conversations; because these three groups interact (e.g., an inhibitor like business-IT governance mismatch can simultaneously suppress assimilation breadth and undermine a success factor like stakeholder commitment), managing them jointly rather than separately gives a more complete, actionable account of how EA artifacts translate into realized organizational value.
operationalization_hint: When diagnosing an underperforming EA practice, assess all three factor groups together (current assimilation diversity/breadth/depth, presence/absence of the five success factors, and presence/absence of the seven inhibitors) rather than addressing only the most visible symptom.
rationale: The grounded-theory model identifies assimilation, success factors, and inhibitors as three interacting groups that influence artifact creation/use and recommends considering them together.

4.4 Factors affecting EA value
We established three groups of factors affecting the value creation potential of EA: EA
practice assimilation, EA practice success factors, and EA practice inhibitors.
4.4.1 EA practice assimilation. An EA practice has a profound impact on an
organization. However, the profoundness depends on the diversity, breadth, and depth
of the assimilation of the EA practice (Hal en et al., 2014; Hazen et al., 2017; Jusuf and
Kurnia, 2017; Kurnia et al., 2021; Pattij et al., 2020). First, the diversity aspect of
assimilation “refers to the amount of differing IT and business processes and
relationships that the EA affects” (Hazen et al., 2017, p. 568). Next, the breadth aspect
“describes how widely the EA is used over the entire organization, that is, how many
functional areas, intra-organizational, and even inter-organizational teams and groups

readiness_statement: The organization proactively screens for seven documented EA-practice inhibitors before or during EA value-realization efforts: (1) business-IT governance mismatch (e.g., centralized IT vs. decentralized business, hierarchical stratification blocking architect access to senior executives); (2) lack of common terminology/communication skills between architects and business; (3) cultural resistance (e.g., EA perceived as legislatively mandated rather than genuinely valuable, business leaders reluctant to negotiate with architects); (4) financial/budget-transparency factors; (5) insufficient business/IT leadership sponsorship; (6) organizational instability (frequent leadership rotation, constant organizational flux); and (7) a troublesome EA history/reputation that demotivates EA staff and stakeholders alike.
mechanism: Each inhibitor independently degrades a specific mechanism EA value depends on: governance mismatch blocks strategic engagement; poor terminology prevents mutual understanding; cultural resistance and instability undermine the sustained stakeholder relationships EA requires; funding opacity and weak sponsorship remove the resources and authority needed to enforce EA compliance -- so screening for all seven, rather than assuming EA failure has one root cause, is necessary for accurate diagnosis.
operationalization_hint: Before launching or troubleshooting an EA initiative, explicitly check for each of the seven inhibitor categories rather than assuming EA underperformance stems from a single generic cause like "lack of buy-in."
rationale: The synthesis details governance mismatch, terminology/communication problems, cultural resistance, funding opacity, weak sponsorship, instability, and troublesome EA history as distinct inhibitors of EA artifact value creation and use.

readiness_statement: The organization classifies its EA artifacts by type -- considerations (general-direction principles), standards (technical reference models for new initiatives), visions (long-term future-state agreements like reference architectures), landscapes (as-is views like context diagrams), outlines (business-leader-understandable conceptual designs of proposed initiatives), and designs (developer-actionable detailed solution architectures) -- to clarify which artifact type is appropriate for which decision-making purpose.
mechanism: Different EA value mechanisms map to different artifact types (e.g., "landscape" artifacts support complexity control and compliance assessment, while "outline" artifacts support stakeholder communication and change-initiative prioritization); without this classification, organizations conflate different artifact purposes and misjudge what a given artifact can or cannot support.
operationalization_hint: When creating or requesting an EA artifact, first identify which of the six artifact types is needed for the decision at hand (e.g., a "vision" for long-term agreement vs. a "design" for developer implementation) rather than producing a generic, undifferentiated "architecture document."

spans.source_excerpt:
4.2 The creation and use of EA artifacts
The creation and use of EA artifacts lead to either of the six types of EA artifacts:
considerations, standards, visions, landscapes, outlines, and designs (Kotusev et al., 2020).
Considerations are EA artifacts that provide general directions defining global architectural
decisions, such as principles. Standards EA artifacts offer technical standards for designing
new change initiatives, such as a technology reference model. Visions are EA artifacts that
provide decisions regarding the organization’s long-term future, agreed upon by business
and IT stakeholders, such as reference architectures. Landscapes are EA artifacts that
provide some objective view of the current organizing logic of business and IT, such as a
context diagram. Outlines are EA artifacts providing conceptual decisions of proposed
change initiatives that are understandable to business leaders, such as a solution overview.
Finally, design EA artifacts offer detailed descriptions of change initiatives, actionable for
developers, such as a complete solution architecture. Specifying the types of different
artifacts offers guidance for the practical usage of EA artifacts (Kotusev et al., 2020).

mechanism: A layer can have many affected elements (high impact) but low interdependency (safe to change incrementally), or fewer affected elements but high interdependency (risky, requires simultaneous coordinated change); conflating these two dimensions into a single "impact" score would hide this important distinction between change volume and change coordination risk.
operationalization_hint: When assessing a strategic initiative's readiness for implementation, report both impact (how many elements/relations are affected) and average intra-relation weight (how tightly those elements depend on each other) as separate readiness indicators.
page_or_section: Section "Evaluation of the Impact of a Strategic Initiative"
rationale: The model defines average intra-relation weight separately from impact and explains that a high value signals tightly dependent components that must operate simultaneously and create greater alignment risk.

mechanism: Business cases built without systematic IT-dependency discovery routinely underestimate scope, cost, and timeline because they miss integration dependencies (e.g., with adjacent business capabilities), dependencies on separately-running initiatives, and pre-existing process debt that must be resolved before digitalization -- all of which the footprinting methodology's gradual capability/system decomposition is specifically designed to surface early.
operationalization_hint: Before finalizing a business case for a digital initiative, walk the affected value-stream steps through progressively deeper heatmapped decomposition (value stream -> business capabilities -> supporting IT systems -> system capability gap analysis) with business and IT stakeholders together, rather than estimating cost/timeline from the business side alone.

readiness_statement: The organization extends the standard three-layer EAM model (business, application, technology) with two additional layers to plan Industry 4.0 transformations: an Operational Layer (production processes, I4.0 components, and sensors, modeled at an abstract/type level rather than instance level, connected to all three standard layers) and an External Interface Layer (partner systems and customers directly involved in production, enabling horizontal integration) -- because the growing similarity between production machines and IT applications (shared security/update/release-management requirements) makes it impossible to cleanly separate operational technology (OT) from business IT within the traditional three layers.
mechanism: As OT and IT converge (production machines increasingly resemble IT applications in their management requirements), traditional EA layers cannot represent the interdependencies enterprise architects need for I4.0 impact analysis (e.g., which business capability depends on which production sensor); adding an Operational Layer as a bridge -- modeled abstractly by type rather than by instance to keep it tractable for architects -- lets the operational department maintain detailed OT models separately while still connecting them to the EA for holistic planning.
operationalization_hint: When planning an Industry 4.0 transformation, explicitly model an Operational Layer (production processes/I4.0 components/sensors, at the type level) connected to business, application, and technology layers, plus an External Interface Layer capturing partner/customer touchpoints in the production process.

raw_condition_label: EA resilience as a distinct organizational-readiness condition alongside EA maturity and digital-transformation maturity
readiness_statement: The organization designs its Enterprise Architecture with explicit resilience measures -- the ability to identify and assess vulnerabilities of enterprise resources in the integrated architecture, prepare for disruptions, adapt to new/changing circumstances, and restore full capability after an unexpected disruption -- as a distinct condition from (but hypothesized to be positively influenced by) general EA maturity and digital transformation maturity.
mechanism: Traditional EA maturity models assess process/practice sophistication but not specifically the organization's capacity to anticipate, absorb, and recover from disruptions (e.g., pandemic-driven supply/demand shocks); explicitly designing "resilience by design" into EA artifacts (a paradigm borrowed from civil engineering post-Hurricane-Sandy) is hypothesized to be a distinguishable, EA-maturity-dependent capability rather than an automatic byproduct of EA maturity.
operationalization_hint: When assessing organizational readiness for disruption, evaluate EA resilience as a separate dimension from EA maturity, using resilience-specific attributes (diversity, redundancy, adaptability, flexibility, agility, vulnerability-to-risk, responsiveness) rather than assuming general EA maturity implies resilience.
rationale: The pilot study defines EA resilience as the capacity to identify and assess vulnerabilities and develops a resilience measurement instrument and conceptual model distinct from general EA and digital-transformation maturity constructs.

2.4. EA Resilience
To the best of our knowledge, Aldea et al. [4] were
the first to coin the term EA resilience and to provide a
definition for it, namely:
EA resilience is the ability of an organization to
identify and assess the vulnerabilities of enterprise
resources in its integrated architecture and prepare for
disruptions, by designing specific measures in an EA to
increase its capabilities to adapt to new or changing
circumstances and restore full capability after an
unexpected disruption.
Bemthuis et al. [20], present another view on EA
resilience by studying it from the perspective of cyber-
physical systems of systems and emergent behaviors.
Additionally, the authors coin the term Enterprise
resilience as a type of resilience that can be facilitated
by designing EA models.
The idea of resilience by design is relatively new
and it originates from the field of civil engineering.
After the disaster brought on by Hurricane Sandy, the
US Department of Housing and Urban Development
proposed a new way to address the structural and
environmental vulnerabilities exposed by the hurricane
and to develop solutions that could provide better
protection from natural events [21]. Thus, according to
Linkov et al. [22], the resilience by design paradigm
defines that a system must be designed to recover its
functions from disruption on its own or else the system
will fail. In terms of EA, this would translate to the idea
that the EA of an organization must be designed with
resilience in mind.
Regarding the attributes and strategies for EA
resilience, Aldea et al. [4] argue that all of the ones
identified for IS resilience might be suitable for EA as
well. However, the authors only theorize this and do not
provide any validation of their assumption. In our
current paper, we aim to address this issue by designing
a survey questionnaire that includes several items
regarding the suitabilityofthese attributes andstrategies
for EA resilience.

2.7. Conceptual Model of EA Resilience in the
context of Digital Transformation
Based on the literature from Sections 2.1 – 2.6, we
have formulated a conceptual model to structure our
research. In this model we have included three core
concepts, namely:

raw_condition_label: EA resilience strategies organized across three temporal phases (Readiness, Responsiveness, Recovery)
readiness_statement: The organization's EA resilience strategies are catalogued and applied according to which of three temporal phases they address: Readiness (preparation before a disturbance, e.g., creating a disruption-management culture, forecasting and risk assessment), Responsiveness (actions during a disruption, e.g., acceptance of consequences, revision of systems, postponement of decision-making), and Recovery (actions after a disruption, e.g., collaboration with stakeholders, knowledge management, sense-making).
mechanism: Different resilience actions are appropriate at different points in a disruption's lifecycle; forecasting/risk-assessment activities (Readiness) address a fundamentally different need than mid-crisis system revision (Responsiveness) or post-crisis sense-making (Recovery), so cataloguing strategies by temporal phase lets an organization identify gaps in its resilience posture across the full disruption lifecycle rather than only preparing for one phase.
operationalization_hint: When assessing EA resilience preparedness, inventory which of the 33 known resilience strategies (per Ramezani & Camarinha-Matos' classification) the organization currently applies in each of the three phases (Readiness/Responsiveness/Recovery), and treat phases with no strategies as priority gaps.
rationale: The paper explicitly adopts Ramezani and Camarinha-Matos' 33-strategy classification, organized into Readiness, Responsiveness, and Recovery, and provides representative actions for each phase.

readiness_statement: The organization treats Alignment and Communication as the two central, interconnected EA-effectiveness constructs that mediate the effect of the other four constructs (Governance, Scope, Top Leadership Commitment, Skilled Teams/Training/Education) -- e.g., top leadership commitment must be communicated to be effective, governance requires communicated roles/responsibilities, and skilled teams need communication skills to translate business requirements into EA -- rather than treating all six constructs as independent, equally-weighted factors.
mechanism: A synthesis of five independent EA-effectiveness measurement approaches found that Alignment and Communication were the three common elements shared across all of them (alongside Scope), and an 11-expert Delphi-style validation confirmed direct or indirect relationships flowing from these two constructs to the other four -- meaning interventions that improve communication or alignment have leveraged, multiplicative effects on the other constructs, rather than each construct needing separate, independent improvement.
operationalization_hint: When diagnosing low EA effectiveness, prioritize improving Alignment and Communication first, since the synthesis model shows these two constructs mediate (are prerequisite to) governance, scope clarity, leadership commitment translating into action, and skilled-team effectiveness.
rationale: The synthesis identifies Alignment, Communication, and Scope as shared elements across five approaches, models Alignment and Communication as connected to the other constructs, and reports confirmation of six constructs by eleven EA experts.

raw_condition_label: EA scope construct (as-is documentation, IT strategy, to-be architecture, transition plan) as a distinct measurable effectiveness construct
readiness_statement: The organization defines EA project scope by producing four specific artifacts: as-is documentation showing the current architecture status, an IT strategy, a target ("to-be") architecture, and a plan for reaching the to-be architecture from the as-is state -- with the scope documentation also stating the anticipated benefits of the EA effort -- rather than leaving "scope" as an informal, undocumented understanding.
mechanism: Without explicit as-is/to-be/transition-plan documentation, an EA effort lacks a defined boundary and cannot be evaluated for completeness or progress; scoping is identified across multiple independent CSF frameworks (Bricknall et al., Ylimäki, Wan et al.) as a recurring, distinct success factor precisely because organizations frequently start EA modeling before defining these boundary artifacts.
operationalization_hint: Before beginning EA modeling work, produce and get sign-off on four scope artifacts: as-is documentation, IT strategy statement, to-be target architecture, and a transition plan between them.
rationale: The synthesized Scope construct explicitly includes benefits, as-is documentation, IT strategy, target architecture, and a plan for reaching the target architecture.

raw_condition_label: absorptive capacity requires deliberate filtering, not maximal absorption, of sensed signals
readiness_statement: The organization deliberately balances its "absorptive capacity" (the ability to recognize the value of new external information, assimilate it, and apply it commercially) against the cost of scanning and analyzing every captured signal, rather than attempting to absorb and act on all detected trends -- explicitly avoiding "blind imitation" of competitors and instead finding its own equilibrium between resources, investments, risks, and the internal/external knowledge enablers it monitors.
mechanism: In a VUCA (volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous) environment, knowledge has a quick time-to-obsolescence, and scanning/analyzing every captured data point can be highly expensive without certain payoff; treating sensing as a continuous listening process rather than an "absorb everything" mandate lets the organization increase context/self-awareness while still being selective about which signals warrant an architecture response.
operationalization_hint: When designing a sensing capability, define explicit filtering/prioritization criteria (e.g., ranking by threat to current portfolio, as in the illustrative case) rather than instrumenting maximal data collection without a corresponding assessment/triage step.
rationale: The paper explicitly argues that scanning every signal is costly and uncertain, defines absorptive capacity, and recommends continuous filtering and rapid decision-making to balance resources, investment, risk, and knowledge enablers.

title: Enterprise Architecture Governance of Excellence
paper_authors: Hillmann, P.; Kesseler, M.; Schnell, D.; Mihelcic, G.; Karcher, A.
authors: Hillmann, P.; Kesseler, M.; Schnell, D.; Mihelcic, G.; Karcher, A.
raw_condition_label: federated enterprise architecture governance requires explicit structural components to coordinate horizontal and vertical EA collaboration
readiness_statement: A federated (multi-business-unit/multi-segment) organization establishes segment-level EA staff units (each supporting its own segment while coordinating with the parent enterprise and sibling segments), a small set of cross-segment governance boards (an EA Blueprint Board for methodology/standards, an EAM Board & Strategy Council for strategic direction, and an EA Portfolio Board for project/investment prioritization, each capped at ~7 members), and a defined role hierarchy (Enterprise Manager, EA Sponsor, EA Governor, EA Portfolio Manager, EA Subject Manager, EA Solution Architect, EA Designer, EA Analyst, EA Method Specialist, EA Repository Administrator) -- rather than relying on informal, ad hoc coordination between autonomous business units.
mechanism: Federated enterprises face inter-dependencies between business units (shared resources like HR/finance, reused sub-products between units) that cannot be coordinated through hierarchy alone when units are peers (horizontal, same-level relationships) rather than parent-child (vertical, hierarchical); explicit boards provide the venue for negotiated, non-hierarchical coordination while segment-level EA staff units provide the local capacity to actually implement agreed standards, with a capped board size (≤7) preventing the ineffectiveness of oversized decision-making bodies.
operationalization_hint: When establishing EA governance for a multi-business-unit conglomerate, distinguish vertical coordination (parent-segment, resolved via hierarchical boards/directives) from horizontal coordination (peer-segment, resolved via negotiated interfaces supported by each segment's EA staff unit) and staff a Portfolio Manager role to coordinate cross-cutting project/resource dependencies.
rationale: The federated-governance concept distinguishes horizontal and vertical coordination, assigns local EA staff capacity, and defines three boards with capped membership and distinct methodology, strategy, and portfolio functions.

raw_condition_label: 10 core EA governance principles as a practical governance foundation
readiness_statement: The organization establishes and maintains fewer than 30 EA principles per governance area, including at minimum: (1) EA pursues value creation evident in every deliverable; (2) stakeholders are identified before any EA artifact is designed; (3) every EA artifact has a clearly stated maturity level; (4) every EA artifact is self-contained; (5) every design follows Service-Oriented-Architecture principles with clearly defined interfaces; (6) standards, reference designs, and glossaries are used extensively; (7) every EA artifact has an identified owner; (8) artifacts follow proper modeling/visualization guidelines; (9) a culture of digital information transfer is established; and (10) a culture welcoming innovation and improvement suggestions is established.
mechanism: Without an explicit, bounded principle set (kept under ~30 per area to remain usable), federated EA governance risks either paralysis (too many competing rules) or inconsistency (no shared rules at all); documenting each principle with ID/Name/Statement/Rationale/Implication (per standard EA-principle practice) and capping the set size keeps the principles both comprehensive and practically enforceable.
operationalization_hint: Draft EA governance principles using the ID/Statement/Rationale/Implication format, cap each governance area at under 30 principles, and explicitly include ownership (principle 7) and stakeholder-identification (principle 2) as non-negotiable baseline principles.
rationale: The paper recommends a bounded principle set, documents the ID/Name/Statement/Rationale/Implication format, and specifies the substantive collaborative-governance principles used in its concept.

raw_condition_label: TOGAF's Requirements Management and Architecture Board provide no guidance for non-hierarchical decision-making authority
readiness_statement: When adopting TOGAF (or a similar centralized-by-default EA framework) in a non-centralized organizational structure, the organization must explicitly recognize and compensate for two specific gaps: (1) the Requirements Management phase gives no guidance on how to collect and prioritize requirements emerging from multiple autonomous sources (only that prioritization should follow "the architecture vision," which itself presumes a single, agreed vision); and (2) the Architecture Board concept presumes a small (4-5 member), top-management-mandated group able to enforce compliance, which has no counterpart in an organization where authority is legitimately distributed.
mechanism: Frameworks such as TOGAF were originally developed assuming centralized IT/management, so their governance and requirements-management guidance implicitly requires a single locus of decision authority; applying them unmodified to federated or decentralized organizations reproduces governance and decision-making irregularities rather than resolving them, because there genuinely is no party empowered to play the assumed centralized role.
operationalization_hint: Before adopting a mainstream EA framework (TOGAF, FEA, etc.) in a federated or decentralized organization, explicitly audit the framework's governance and requirements-management guidance for hidden centralization assumptions, and design a compensating multi-party governance mechanism rather than assuming the framework's default guidance will transfer.
rationale: The case analysis identifies TOGAF's implicit centralization assumptions: requirements prioritization is only tied to one architecture vision and the recommended 4–5 member Board lacks authority and representation in autonomous federations.

enterprise-wide organizational viewpoint, this approach of working is not feasible nor

title: Product-IT Inclusive Enterprise Architecture Management: An Approach Based on Ecosystems, Customer Journey and Data-Driven Business Opportunities
paper_authors: Kaidalova, J.; Sandkuhl, K.; Seigerroth, U.
authors: Kaidalova, J.; Sandkuhl, K.; Seigerroth, U.
raw_condition_label: product-IT inclusive EA extends enterprise-IT-only architecture with product-centric concepts to represent smart, connected products
readiness_statement: The organization extends its Enterprise Architecture meta-model (built on ArchiMate) with product-centric concepts -- Offering (products/services combined for value creation), Ecosystem (an offering or group of offerings plus their key actors), Touchpoint (customer interaction channels, pre/purchase/post-purchase), Experience (the actor's subjective response to an interaction), Concern (an actor's problem/need), and Technology Area (a domain of IT-intensive methods/solutions) -- so that smart, connected products (which combine physical, "smart," and connectivity components) are represented within the same EA alongside traditional enterprise-IT elements, rather than being modeled in a separate, disconnected product-development silo.
mechanism: As physical products increasingly embed software, sensors, and connectivity ("product-IT"), traditional EA models (which capture only enterprise-IT: business/data/application/technology layers) miss the substantial IT content now residing inside the product itself, causing duplicated architecture effort and missed integration opportunities (e.g., shared encryption/logging services needed by both product software and enterprise software); explicitly extending the EA meta-model with product-facing concepts closes this representational gap so both product-IT and enterprise-IT can be jointly planned and aligned.
operationalization_hint: When a product line is undergoing (or has undergone) digitization/connectivity additions, extend the EA meta-model to explicitly include Offering/Ecosystem/Touchpoint/Experience/Concern/Technology-Area concepts, and use the three method components (ecosystem-of-offerings mapping, customer-journey mapping, data-driven-business-options mapping) during Business Architecture development (TOGAF ADM phases B/C) to surface product-IT integration needs early.

cluster_label: Modeling foundations for traceability & automated alignment
rationale: The product-IT-inclusive approach extends an ArchiMate-based meta-model with product-facing concepts and applies ecosystem, customer-journey, and data-driven-business-option method components, which were evaluated with industrial and academic experts.

spans.source_excerpt:
For some of the extensions, there are concepts in ArchiMate that could have been used to
represent them, e.g., ArchiMate’s “business collaboration” to model “ecosystem” or ArchiMate’s
“driver” to model “concern”. However, the semantics of Ecosystem and Concern is slightly
different from Business collaboration and Driver, which supported the decision in favor of the
extensions.
5.3 Selected Method Components
Based on the concept model in previous section we have selected three method components for
further presentation, namely, ecosystem of offerings, customer journey and data-driven business
options. The main reason for the selection of these three method components is that they are the
method components that cater for bridging the gap between product-IT and enterprise-IT and to
make EAM product-IT inclusive. The presentation of the method components follows the same
structure for each method component: we start with the concepts from the meta-model (see
Section 5.2) of particular importance to the method components, which is followed by a brief
description of the objective of the method component. Subsequently, an example from the case
study presented in Section 4.1 is given and the procedure to follow within the method component
is summarized.

Procedures: The procedure for modeling of ecosystem of offerings includes five steps and is
based on the concepts that define this focal area (Figure 9).
Figure 9. Procedures for modeling of ecosystem of offerings
1. Set the scope for analysis and identify the offerings that are important within the chosen
scope. The offerings can be tangible or intangible, e.g., services, products or other value
adding things. After the offerings are identified, group them. Each of the created groups
correspond to an ecosystem of offerings. Set a suitable name for each ecosystem based on
the character of the included offerings.

--- PAGE 17 ---
17
2. Identify the important actors. They can include stakeholders that contribute into providing
the key offerings or play other important roles in the given ecosystem. For instance, you can
consider competitors, trend setting players on the market, providers of the competence or
technological solutions, providers of the relevant information or data, customer groups,
potential partners. Actors can be individuals, groups of people or other communicating
entities.
3. Represent the actors and their relationships. For this, analyze collaborative, competitive and
other types of relationships between the identified actors.
4. Consider and identify the concerns that the actors have. For this, analyze incentives and
pain points (general or detailed) of the identified actors. List the concerns and relate them to
the identified ecosystems. Analyze which concerns can be resolved with the help of the
existing offerings from the identified ecosystems, and which ones remain unresolved and
can provide basis for new offerings and ecosystems.
5. Review and refine.

6 Validation of Approach and Selected Method Components
The presented method components and the approach as a whole were validated through semi-
structured interviews with experts. The validation was divided into three evaluation meetings as
discussed below.
Evaluation meeting 1 with two experts
This activity was designed to evaluate the concepts for product-IT inclusive EA. The descriptive
evaluation through informed argument and scenarios in combination with evaluation through
structural testing were applied. The set of concepts for Product-IT inclusive EA was
demonstrated to the invited expert and discussed in detail. The concept model, see Figure 4
above, was presented, together with arguments for introducing new concepts. A number of
scenarios was suggested, and the expert validated whether the proposed set of scenarios was
sufficient to cover the domain in focus. Afterwards, the relationships between the specified
concepts were validated, which served as a structural testing of the concept model in represented
in Figure 4. Suggestions for improvements were documented and implemented through revision
of the conceptual model(s).
Experts: two industrial experts in EA and digital product development, digital transformation
and human-centered design.
Key contributions: evaluated set of concepts for product-IT inclusive EA.
Evaluation meeting 2 with one expert
This activity was designed to evaluate several dimensions of the product-IT inclusive EA
approach: Concepts for product-IT inclusive EA, Focal areas for product-IT inclusive EA,
Stakeholders for product-IT inclusive EA and Method for product-IT inclusive EA as a whole.
The approach with these components was presented to the invited experts and discussed in detail.
The descriptive evaluation was performed through presentation of scenarios together with
arguments for each scenario. The expert evaluated whether the suggested set of concepts was
sufficient to cover the domain in focus. In this evaluation meeting a set of stakeholders was also
presented and discussed in detail with regards to the responsibilities and organizational
affiliations. Suggestions for the improvements were documented and implemented in the
method. The method was also validated in terms of structural coherence. The method component
constituents were discussed with a special focus on the relationships between them. The method
structure was also discussed in relation to the existing methods in EA field, comparing the aims
of the methods and the choice of the method constituents to satisfy these aims.
Expert: industrial expert in Enterprise-IT implementation and integration, broad experience
on digital transformation and shift from physical product production to smart, connected product
production in traditional manufacturing companies.
Key contributions: validated set of concepts, focal areas and stakeholders for product-IT
inclusive EA.

inclusive EA.

7 Conclusions
Based on an industrial case that illustrates the development of smart connected products and the
creation of new kinds of business services, this article derives requirements for a product-IT
inclusive EAM approach and addresses method support for product-IT inclusive business and
application architectures. As a foundation for the method support, a meta-model is proposed
which builds upon ArchiMate and integrates additional concepts required for representing
product-IT and its use. The method as such consists of various components addressing the focal
areas ecosystem of offerings, customer journey and data-driven business services. This method
support can be integrated into TOGAF ADM in the phases B (Business Architecture) and C
(Information Systems Architecture).
Application of the proposed method on two industrial cases showed its applicability and
usefulness. One of the cases is included in this article in Section 4.1; and the excerpts from the
case as examples are shown when introducing the method components in Section 5.3. Detailed
information about the second case is included in [22]. Furthermore, expert evaluation confirmed
that the method meets industrial demands.

--- PAGE 24 ---
24
Future work will concern empirical and conceptulal perspectives. From an empirical
perspective, application of the method in additional cases should be in focus to gain experiences
and additional requirements for improving or revising the method. Application cases should
primarily be enterprises with smart connected products. Other application fields with substantial
product-IT should follow to check applicability of the method and adaptation needs. The
conceptual perspective of future work should include the search for additional focal areas and
their integration into the meta-model and method components. Examples could be service
evolution or product-IT prepared for the third party components.

raw_condition_label: bimodal IT governance (stable Mode-1 enterprise-IT vs. agile Mode-2 product-IT) as a structural requirement for product-centric digital transformation
readiness_statement: The organization differentiates its IT governance and delivery model by mode: Mode 1 (enterprise-IT: accounting, finance, HR) is governed for stability, efficiency, and low cost using traditional EAM practices, while Mode 2 (product-IT: embedded/connected product software) is governed for fast turnaround, frequent updates, and high business involvement using DevOps-style teams -- with the enterprise architecture method explicitly required to remain applicable across both coexisting modes rather than assuming a single delivery cadence.
mechanism: Established enterprises (unlike digitally-native startups with a "clean slate") carry years of legacy technology, governance, and financing structures on the enterprise-IT side, while product-IT demands rapid, frequent, business-driven iteration to remain competitive; without an explicit bimodal governance split (and a method that can operate across both), the slower enterprise-IT governance model tends to be applied to product-IT by default, throttling the innovation speed the product side needs.
operationalization_hint: When planning digital transformation of a physical-product business, classify system/architecture components as Mode 1 (enterprise-IT, stability-governed) or Mode 2 (product-IT, agility-governed) early, and assign differentiated governance cadences (e.g., DevOps teams for Mode 2) rather than applying uniform enterprise-IT governance to both.
rationale: The industrial context explicitly differentiates stable, efficient Mode 1 enterprise-IT from rapid, business-involved Mode 2 product-IT and uses DevOps teams for the latter; the method must operate across both modes.

A challenge that is apparent today in the digital transformation is the ability to handle the bi-

[23] stated that there is a need to handle “A two speed architecture for the digital enterprise”.
For digitally native enterprises and startups this is not a problem, since they have had the benefit
of starting with a “clean slate” and think “digital” and take the advantage of this from the
beginning without considering any legacy. This does, however, not work for more established
enterprises. They have many years of delivered technology, architectures, governance, decisions

differentiate the systems, architectures, and structures that must be flexible and agile (often on

mechanism: Ad hoc or purely case-derived capability lists risk being idiosyncratic to one organization's context and unstable as new capabilities are discovered; grounding the initial map in a broad literature synthesis (1,383 sources here) before case validation, combined with an explicit stability criterion (no top-two-level changes post-validation), produces a capability map robust enough to serve as a shared reference across multiple organizations rather than a one-off artifact.
operationalization_hint: When scoping a digital-twin or Industry 4.0 transformation initiative, first derive a candidate capability list via structured literature review, group it hierarchically (2-5 sub-capabilities per group) by van Riel's generic capability-map method, then validate stability against a real case before treating the top-level structure as fixed.

rationale: The map is derived through an SLR, structured hierarchically, and validated against an explicit no-change-to-top-two-levels stability criterion after industry review; the source reports 1,383 screened sources and 76 capability-bearing results.

readiness_statement: The organization works through a five-step procedure to operationalize a capability map for a transformation initiative: (1) define strategic objectives for the initiative; (2) identify requisite capabilities from the capability map/repository; (3) assess each identified capability's strategic relevance (business impact, alignment, feasibility); (4) conduct a fit-gap analysis distinguishing capabilities that are missing entirely from capabilities that exist but need maturity enhancement; and (5) plan capability realization as a roadmap with milestones informing resource allocation and prioritization.
mechanism: Without a defined procedure connecting strategic objectives to a capability roadmap, capability maps risk being descriptive reference documents that are never operationalized into actual investment decisions; the fit-gap step in particular is necessary because "missing capability" and "immature existing capability" require different remediation actions (build vs. enhance), and conflating them leads to misallocated transformation investment.
operationalization_hint: When using a capability map (Industry-4.0-specific or general-purpose) to plan a transformation initiative, run the five-step procedure explicitly, keeping the fit-gap analysis's two perspectives (missing vs. immature capabilities) as separate roadmap workstreams.
rationale: The capability-based planning procedure connects strategic goals to relevant-capability identification, relevance assessment, fit-gap analysis, and a resource-informing realization roadmap.

raw_condition_label: federated governance balancing centralized standards with decentralized domain autonomy
readiness_statement: A data architecture assigns data ownership and production responsibility to decentralized, domain-oriented teams (each domain independently produces and publishes its own data products, accompanied by a data contract, to a shared Data Product Catalog) while a Federated Governance layer defines and enforces enterprise-wide, non-negotiable standards -- access/compliance/privacy/exchange policies, interoperability (technical and semantic) requirements, and documentation policy -- that all domains must follow regardless of their operational autonomy, with a Self-Serve Data Platform providing the shared infrastructure (storage, query engines, access control, ETL) domains use to implement these standards themselves.
mechanism: Fully centralized, monolithic data architectures create bottlenecks (central teams cannot keep pace with all domains' data needs, causing low domain-specific knowledge and long lead times), while fully decentralized data ownership without any shared governance risks incompatible standards, data duplication, and siloed, non-interoperable data products; federating governance (shared, enforceable policies) while decentralizing production (domain-owned data products) captures the scalability benefit of decentralization without sacrificing enterprise-wide consistency and security.
operationalization_hint: When designing a data architecture for a large, multi-domain organization, model three explicit ArchiMate layers -- Domain-Driven Data-as-Product, Self-Serve Data Platform, Federated Governance -- and ensure the governance layer's policies (access, compliance, privacy, exchange, interoperability, documentation) are enforced identically across all domains regardless of each domain's operational autonomy.

raw_condition_label: data mesh archetypes (fully-federated, fully-governed, hybrid, value-chain/coarse-grained) as a centralization-decentralization spectrum organizations select by context
readiness_statement: An organization selects its data mesh implementation from a spectrum of archetypes rather than assuming full decentralization is always the goal: a fine-grained fully-federated mesh (maximum domain autonomy and specialization, but capability duplication/cost/complexity risk), a fully-governed mesh (a central data-distribution layer improving compliance at the cost of flexibility), a hybrid federated mesh (middle ground, simplified management with some overhead), and value-chain-aligned/coarse-grained meshes (suited to complex supply chains or post-merger organizations with larger, less granular domain boundaries).
mechanism: No single data mesh archetype solves all organizational data challenges; an organization's appropriate degree of federation depends on factors such as its number and boundary-clarity of business domains, its M&A history, and its supply-chain complexity, so treating "data mesh" as a single fixed target architecture (rather than a spectrum to select from) risks over- or under-decentralizing relative to organizational needs.
operationalization_hint: Before committing to a data mesh implementation, explicitly assess organizational factors (domain boundary clarity, M&A/supply-chain complexity, data literacy/technical-expertise levels) against the four archetypes to select the appropriate degree of federation rather than defaulting to the most decentralized (fully-federated) form.
rationale: The systematic review identifies a context-dependent spectrum of fine-grained federated, governed, hybrid, value-chain-aligned, and coarse-grained data-mesh archetypes, each with distinct autonomy, complexity, and centralization trade-offs.

3.2 Data Mesh Archetypes and Components
This subsection explores the main archetypes of data meshes, their components,
and the limitations they present [8].
Data mesh architectures, though ﬂexible, typically consist of key compo-
nents necessary for eﬀective implementation. These include domains, a self-serve
data platform, and a federated governance layer [23]. However, data meshes
are not a one-size-ﬁts-all solution, and their structure can vary signiﬁcantly
between organizations. Various topologies have been identiﬁed in existing lit-
erature, ranging from a ﬁne-grained, fully decentralized mesh to more managed,
centralized forms. Importantly, a data mesh’s speciﬁc archetype depends on an
organization’s requirements, and no single archetype solves all organizational
data challenges [14].
The ﬁrst archetype, a ﬁne-grained fully federated mesh, represents the most
theoretical and decentralized form of a data mesh, where each domain oper-
ates independently, handling its own data and communication. While oﬀering
high ﬂexibility and domain specialization, this approach poses challenges, such
as capability duplication, high costs, and complexity. The fully governed mesh,
another variation, introduces a central data distribution layer to tackle some of
these issues. In this model, domains retain autonomy, but data distribution is
controlled through a central layer, improving compliance at the cost of ﬂexibility.
The hybrid federated mesh oﬀers a middle ground, combining both centralized
and decentralized elements, thus simplifying management but adding some over-
head [23].
A variety of other archetypes also exist, such as the value-chain aligned and
coarse-grained meshes, which are suitable for organizations with diﬀerent opera-
tional models, such as those involved in complex supply chains or those that have

raw_condition_label: EA-grounded sense-making, knowledge-creation, and decision-making (Knowing Cycle) as the process linking baseline-architecture assessment to target-architecture transformation initiatives
readiness_statement: The organization structures its EA-driven transformation process explicitly through Choo's three-mode Knowing Cycle: sense-making (bracketing raw organizational/environmental data via interviews/workshops, interpreting it to produce the current-state/baseline architecture and an architecture vision), knowledge creation (converting stakeholder-shared tacit knowledge into explicit architectural artifacts stored in an EA repository, modeling the target/to-be architecture), and decision-making (using the created knowledge to identify, develop, and select transformation initiatives that close the gap between baseline and target architecture) -- rather than treating architecture development as a purely technical modeling exercise disconnected from organizational knowledge processes.
mechanism: EA artifacts (models, repositories) are themselves a form of organizational knowledge, and the process of producing them mirrors the general organizational knowing cycle (making sense of a changing environment, creating new knowledge to address it, deciding how to act); making this connection explicit lets architects deliberately manage the sense-making step (contextualizing stakeholder input) as a precondition for knowledge creation, rather than treating architecture documentation as a standalone deliverable.
operationalization_hint: When running an EA-driven transformation, explicitly stage the work as sense-making (interviews/workshops to build the current-state model and architecture vision) -> knowledge creation (converting stakeholder tacit knowledge into target-architecture artifacts in a managed repository) -> decision-making (deriving and selecting prioritized transformation initiatives from the baseline-target gap).

rationale: The proposed framework explicitly connects sense-making, knowledge creation, and decision-making to baseline/target architecture work, repositories, and the selection of transformation initiatives.

raw_condition_label: organizational technology-adoption maturity requires balanced advancement across both technical and organizational/business-model dimensions
readiness_statement: An organization adopting a new architectural/technology paradigm (here, microservices) assesses and advances its readiness along two distinct dimensions in tandem -- technical maturity (API design, service discovery, authentication, performance monitoring, orchestration sophistication) and organizational maturity (talent/hiring, licensing/monetization model, management buy-in, business-model realignment) -- since observed organizations rarely show a high level of maturity on one dimension while remaining low on the other, and full paradigm benefits require both to progress together.
mechanism: Technical implementation of a new architectural style (e.g., building working microservices) is necessarily visible and easy to observe, biasing organizational attention and investment toward the technical dimension; but the paradigm's business value (agility, new revenue models, faster time-to-market) depends equally on organizational changes (talent, licensing, business-model shift) that are less visible and easier to neglect, so tracking only technical maturity produces a false sense of overall transformation readiness.
operationalization_hint: When assessing readiness to adopt a new architectural/technology paradigm, score both a technical-maturity dimension and an organizational-maturity dimension (each on the same level scale) rather than a single combined or technical-only score, and treat a large gap between the two dimensions as a specific risk flag.
page_or_section: Sections 3.1-3.3 (Maturity Levels, Maturity Dimensions, Technical/Organizational Maturity Dimension)
rationale: The Microservice Maturity Model applies five levels across technical and organizational dimensions, describes organizational business-model realignment, and reports that large cross-dimension maturity gaps are rarely observed.

The levels of maturity defined in the previous section can serve as a framework for

raw_condition_label: Frame & Work Module (F&WM) modularization operationalizes the sensing-seizing-transforming dynamic-capability cycle into concrete steps executives can follow to understand digital transformation
readiness_statement: The organization decomposes its business architecture into modules (What: modularization, KPIs, strengths; Who: customers; How: business model) and works through five concrete steps -- (1) decompose business processes into modules, (2) quantify each module via KPIs, (3) identify module strengths from the KPI data, (4) identify the most valuable customer segment for those strengths, (5) sense/seize/transform to develop a new business exploiting that strength -- so that non-technical executives (who understand overall business architecture but often lack digital-era experience) can follow a concrete, step-by-step process rather than relying on the abstract, unspecified "iterative cycle" Teece's dynamic-capabilities theory describes without a reproducible model.
mechanism: Teece's dynamic-capabilities theory asserts the necessity of an iterative sensing-seizing-transforming cycle but (per the paper's own review of Teece and Kikuzawa) does not provide a specific, reproducible model for executing it; decomposing the business into quantifiable modules gives executives concrete artifacts (KPIs, strength profiles) to reason about and discuss, translating an abstract capability-theory prescription into a walkable procedure that bridges the digital-literacy gap between technically inexperienced senior management and DX initiatives.
operationalization_hint: When guiding management through a digital-transformation understanding process, break the business into modules with the F&WM What/Who/How dimensions, quantify each module's current performance via KPIs before attempting any DX intervention, and use the resulting strength/weakness profile to identify which customer segments and business-model changes to pursue next.

rationale: The paper defines the F&WM What, Who, and How dimensions, gives the five step cycle from modularization through a new targeted business, and concludes that the dynamic-capability iteration can be decomposed through these five steps.

raw_condition_label: IO-data-driven, loosely-coupled architecture mapping business processes 1:1 to microservice-style building blocks enables lower-cost, faster architecture refactoring
readiness_statement: The organization designs its Enterprise Information System so that each business process (defined purely by its input and output data) maps directly to one application component and one or more highly-cohesive technology-layer "commands" connected only through data objects (Unix-pipe-style), producing a microservice/loosely-coupled architecture in which business-process analysis and design are simultaneously data-and-application design -- rather than designing business processes, applications, and technology as separate, loosely-synchronized layers.
mechanism: Because each command/component has a single, sophisticated function processing only input/output data, dependencies between components are minimized, letting the organization refactor (re-develop) individual parts of the EIS without cascading changes through the rest of the system; the real-case company achieved measurable multi-year re-development at lower cost specifically because the architecture's loose coupling meant that a single business-process change corresponded to a bounded application-component change rather than a system-wide rewrite.
operationalization_hint: When designing an EIS intended for frequent Agile/Lean-style refactoring, define business processes strictly by their input/output data, map each process 1:1 to an application component built from small, single-function IO-based commands, and connect components only through data objects rather than shared middleware or direct calls.
rationale: The Unicage proposal maps IO-defined business processes to data-linked application components and highly cohesive commands; its case reports lower-cost refactoring, while the paper bounds the method to ERP and calls for further evaluation.

5. Discussion
5.1. Novelty
In the Digital Transformation (DX) era and the current competitive business market, enterprises and their
information systems need to be adaptive to any unpresented event such as Covid-19 [14]. The major enterprise
architecture frameworks such an Open Agile Architecture (O-AA) [4], TOGAF [2], Enterprise Architecture
Planning [EAP] and, Lean and Agile Software Development [6], [13] suggest the enterprises good guidance,
defining a set of deliverables of the guidance or framework. However, this guidance for enterprise information
system architecture is often broad and conceptual which is inevitable to realize higher adoptability for any
enterprise, despite it also sets the enterprises to seek a practical implementation to meet the guidance criteria. Thus,
we proposed the practical building blocks to expand the core architecture layers recommended by TOGAF [3] with
loosely coupled microservice technology architecture along with data and application architecture which especially
fits for Enterprise Resource Planning systems. The novelty here shall be (1) data driven business process design
method which directly maps to (2) loosely-coupled application components constructed with (3) highly cohesive
command modules. The commands as (4) a software cushion also play a decisive role to realize loosely-coupled
application components and the full cycle development [9].
5.2. Effectiveness
The proposed architecture development method has been effectively introduced to the company in the user case
and shown its effectiveness in a quantitative way. It has also shown that the architecture is a microservice or loosely
coupled architecture which has made the architecture refactoring achieve with less cost or effort.
6. Conclusion
In this paper, we proposed the data driven enterprise architecture development method- Unicage Architecture
Development Method (UADM) with the practical implementation blocks with ArchiMate metamodels, expanding
the current enterprise architecture framework guidance. Although the proposed architecture development method
has effectively applied to the case, the architecture is designed for Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), especially.
More quantitative evaluation on its effectiveness shall be conducted and more detailed and methodological
explanation on business architecture be illustrated.
Future work includes more case studies illustrated with the proposed architecture development method.

paper_authors: Elshan, E.; van den Hooff, B.
authors: Elshan, E.; van den Hooff, B.
raw_condition_label: EA governance under decentralized/citizen-development technologies (e.g., low-code platforms) requires a deliberately composed portfolio pairing formal instruments with informal enabling practices, not a single centralization/decentralization choice
readiness_statement: The organization governs emerging, decentralization-enabling technologies (such as Low-Code Development Platforms) by deliberately assembling a portfolio of paired strategy clusters -- e.g., formal application registration + informal community "show and tell" sessions; formal risk-tiered guardrails + informal co-design with citizen developers; formal RACI role definitions + informal architect-to-developer mentoring -- rather than choosing either strict centralized top-down control (which citizen developers experience as bureaucratic, eroding the agility that motivated LCDP adoption) or unstructured decentralized enablement (which produces uncontrolled application proliferation, architectural drift, and security exposure).
mechanism: Across three organizations in different regulated sectors (finance, healthcare, manufacturing), purely centralized governance consistently suppressed the innovation/agility benefit that justified adopting decentralized development platforms in the first place, while purely informal/decentralized governance consistently produced shadow-IT-like proliferation, technical debt, and security exposure; pairing formal instruments (which supply clarity, traceability, and safeguards) with informal practices (which cultivate capability, legitimacy, and shared ownership) is what let all three organizations sustain both architectural coherence and development speed simultaneously.
operationalization_hint: When governing any decentralization-enabling technology (low-code platforms, citizen development, or by extension AI-assisted/agentic development), design governance as an explicit portfolio combining at least one formal instrument (registration, risk tiers, RACI) with at least one informal enabling practice (community sessions, co-design, mentoring) for each governance challenge identified, rather than defaulting to either pure top-down control or pure laissez-faire enablement.
page_or_section: Findings section (Strategies; Discussion and conclusion, "A conceptual model of balanced governance")
rationale: The three-case study finds governance effectiveness in deliberately coupling formal instruments with informal enabling practices, rather than selecting a single centralized/decentralized or formal/informal control mode.

It is important to note that the centralized–
decentralized and formal–informal dimensions of gov­
ernance, while related, are analytically distinct. Cen­
tralized versus decentralized governance concerns the
locus of control: centralized governance concentrates
decision-making authority in a single unit or role—such
as a Chief Architect or central EA ofﬁce—while de­
centralized governance distributes authority across

(Boh and Yellin, 2006; Gregory et al., 2018). Formal
versus informal governance, by contrast, concerns the
mode of control: formal control relies on explicit stan­
dards, performance evaluation, and hierarchical en­
forcement, whereas informal control originates from
intrinsic motivation, self-regulation, and interpersonal
interaction (Beese et al., 2023b; Ouchi, 1979). These two
dimensions are orthogonal: a centralized governance
model may employ informal mechanisms (as when a
Chief Architect builds norms through coaching rather
than mandates), and a decentralized model may use
formal controls (as when distributed business units are

Our ﬁndings show that organizations responded to LCDP
governance challenges not by choosing between these
orientations but by composing portfolios that combined
centralized instruments with informal enabling
practices—a conﬁguration  our data suggest is distinc­

Our ﬁndings show that sustainable governance does not
simply balance these dimensions but rebundles them: the
ﬁve mechanisms constitute a portfolio in which formal and
informal complements operate simultaneously across both
loci, generating outcomes that neither dimension could
produce alone. Our ﬁndings reﬂect precisely this orthog­
onality: the governance portfolios we observed pair cen­
tralizedinstrumentswithinformalenablingpractices,rather
than treating centralization and formalization as a single
axis. Our evidence shows that the introduction of LCDPs
triggers precisely such a recomposition: organizations do
not abandon control so much as rebundle it, pairing rules,
structures and risk-tiered assurance checkpoints with en­
ablement, participation, and community routines. The
contribution of our work, however, goes beyond endorse­
ment of “balance.” We specify how balance works. First,
we conceptualize governance as a formative, adaptive
portfolio rather than a reﬂective set of levers: removing a
component alters the nature of governance rather than
merely weakening it. Second, we identify mechanisms
through which the portfolio takes effect and we show how
outcomes feed back to recalibrate the portfolio over time.
Together, these elements advance portfolio thinking in EA
from a general call for balance (Beese et al., 2023b) to a
mechanism-based theory of how complements among
formal and informal elements generate a durable
governance.

readiness_statement: The organization requires mandatory registration of every citizen-developed application with a minimal documentation set (ownership, data classification, dependencies), conducts periodic audits and scheduled portfolio reviews to retire duplicate/obsolete applications, and complements these formal instruments with informal practices such as lightweight documentation templates and community "show and tell" sessions where teams present what they built -- producing "information symmetry": a shared, accurate, current picture of the application landscape held jointly by architects, governance boards, and citizen developers.
mechanism: Decentralized, citizen-led application development is invisible to central EA/IT by default (applications emerge outside established governance boundaries), and this invisibility -- not citizen development itself -- is the proximate cause of architectural drift, technical debt, and duplicated effort; making the landscape visible via registration and hygiene practices is a prerequisite that "completes the loop" enabling other governance mechanisms (proportionate guardrails, secure-by-default pipelines) to function, since none of them can operate correctly against an undocumented, unknown application inventory.
operationalization_hint: When decentralized/citizen development platforms are introduced, mandate lightweight but non-negotiable application registration (owner, data sensitivity, dependencies) from day one, schedule periodic portfolio reviews to retire redundant applications, and pair these formal requirements with informal show-and-tell/community practices that make documentation a shared norm rather than a compliance burden.
page_or_section: Findings section (Visibility and portfolio hygiene; Mechanisms)
rationale: The cross-case evidence pairs mandatory registration, minimum documentation, audits, portfolio review, templates, and show-and-tell practices, linking them to information symmetry and improved visibility, reuse, and quality.

readiness_statement: The organization designs governance guardrails (standards, review gates, exception procedures) to be transparent (rationale for each rule explicitly communicated), proportionate (control depth scaled to risk, not uniformly strict), and co-designed with citizen developers and business stakeholders through participatory forums and a Center of Excellence that provides rapid, supportive advisory rather than only enforcement -- because when developers perceive governance as arbitrary or purely restrictive, they bypass rules or engage in only superficial compliance, whereas participatory, explained governance is experienced as legitimate and is followed voluntarily.

operationalization_hint: When rolling out governance guardrails for decentralized development, explain the rationale behind each rule (not just the rule itself), scale control depth to actual risk rather than applying uniform maximum scrutiny, and establish a participatory forum (e.g., a Center of Excellence) where citizen developers co-own the standards backlog rather than only receiving it.
page_or_section: Findings section (Governance frameworks and pragmatic guardrails; Center of Excellence and participatory governance; Mechanisms)
rationale: The cases connect transparent, proportionate, participatory guardrails and timely advisory to perceived legitimacy, reduced resistance and workarounds, and voluntary compliance.

readiness_statement: The organization codifies responsibility-accountability (RACI-style) mappings across the full lifecycle of decentralized development (from ideation through retirement), explicitly redefining the role of EA/IT staff from centralized gatekeepers/controllers toward supportive guides who mentor and collaborate with citizen developers -- in one case structurally separating an "enabling" function (platform, tooling, standards, reusable building blocks) from a "delivery" function (actual application development) -- so that ownership is unambiguous both on paper and in day-to-day practice.
mechanism: When decision rights are not explicitly codified, citizen developers gain de facto production capability without corresponding accountability, generating persistent "who owns this now" conflicts between IT, business units, and developers that stall decisions and require repeated escalation to resolve; explicitly redefining and separating the enabling role (owned by EA/IT) from the delivery role (owned by developer teams) resolves this ambiguity structurally rather than relying on ad hoc case-by-case negotiation.
operationalization_hint: When decentralizing development authority to business units or citizen developers, formally separate the "enabling" function (platform/tooling/standards ownership, retained by EA/IT) from the "delivery" function (application development ownership, devolved to business-facing teams), and document a RACI-style decision-rights map spanning the full application lifecycle rather than leaving ownership boundaries implicit.
page_or_section: Findings section (Role redefinition and alignment of decision rights; Mechanisms)
rationale: The role-redefinition cluster formalizes lifecycle responsibilities and shifts EA/IT from gatekeeping to mentoring; the authors report clear ownership reduced decision latency and escalation frequency.
