Basic business assumptions relate to the way in which an
entity’s operations are managed (Boshoff, 2014). Its
implementation is essential in order for an entity to perform
its basic day-to-day tasks efficiently and effectively in its
specific business environment (Boshoff, 2014; Goosen &
Rudman, 2013, p. 95). Basic business assumptions are
expected to be established in every entity and is not unique to
specific entities or industries (Boshoff, 2014). Examples of
basic business assumptions include, inter alia, that all entities
are profit orientated, transact across all business processes,
comply with general laws and regulations applicable to all
entities, and consider cash flow and business continuity to be
of critical importance (Boshoff, 2014; Goosen & Rudman,
2013, p. 95). Basic IT solutions and internal controls are
implemented in order to govern basic business assumptions
(Goosen & Rudman, 2013, p. 95). This, however, does not
constitute business-IT alignment (Boshoff, 2014).
Business imperatives expand beyond the basic business
assumptions and are those essential driving forces which
need to be implemented in an entity and executed
extraordinarily well for an entity to meet its strategic
objectives (Boshoff, 2014). Business imperatives act as the key
driving forces of an entity and the successful execution
thereof will give the entity a competitive advantage in its
specific environment (Boshoff, 2014). Business imperatives
are therefore influenced by the context of an entity and
determines the technology architecture which has to be
governed (Boshoff, 2014).

readiness_statement: Across the case studies (detailed for Case 1, a Dutch national-government body, in Table 5), soft-governance focus areas showed large before/after changes once discussed in interview (e.g. Participation: 10 participants at level A pre-interview dropping to 2 post-interview, with 5 moving to level B and 3 to level C; Understanding & trust: 10 at level A pre-interview dropping to 6), whereas hard-governance focus areas like IT decision-making showed minimal change (9 vs. 8 at level A). Where changes occurred, they were always toward a higher maturity level, never lower.
mechanism: Third-cycle MIG assessment instrument (self-report Likert-scale statements per focus area/maturity level) administered to participants, followed by semi-structured interviews discussing and, where warranted, correcting the self-assessed results; before/after comparison tabulated per focus area across all 10 organizations.
operationalization_hint: When assessing ITG (or any governance) maturity via self-report instruments, treat soft-governance/behavioral results as provisional until validated through structured follow-up interviews -- hard-governance/structural self-assessments can be trusted with less follow-up verification, but soft-governance self-assessments routinely under- or over-state maturity until participants receive clarification on what each level actually means.
rationale: Case-1 results directly show larger interview adjustments for soft than hard governance and explain that clarification changed some ratings. The broader claim is best read as evidence from the instrument's case studies.

deficiencies. We conclude that a combination of the MIG assessment instrument and structured interviews is useful for
measuring current hard and soft ITG.

6.1 Limitations
The case studies described in this paper are conducted in the Netherlands and the in-depth case studies were in
government organizations. The case studies show that it is possible to use the intrument to map the current ITG of an
organization into the MIG model. The investigated organizations differ in terms of size and industrial sector. However,
the evaluation was limited to organizations based in the Netherlands and large multinationals, which vary in size and
industrial sector. Case studies in other countries or regions with different cultures might deliver different results.

The evaluation in this study indicate that the MIG instrument continues to require improvements, and this will require
several cycles. We conducted case studies with relatively few participants (between three and 10). All cases studies
described in this paper were conducted in the Netherlands. It would be interesting to conduct case studies with a larger
number of participants or use and validate the model in other countries.
The MIG instrument was created in Excel. An online version of the instrument would be easier to use and represent a
good way of creating a case study database that might be usable to create benchmarks. Further improvements to the
questionnaire might help achieve the ultimate goal: to create an instrument that can be used by the members of an
organization without requiring interviews to correct the results and render the instrument available to the public.

4.2. Choices necessary for the implementation
The current publications on the MIG model do not contain a clear description of the model, which should be used
for the focus area “informal organization”.
Three alternatives have been suggested: Variables outlined by Cobb56
, seven types of lateral relations developed
by Galbraith57
and the Sociogram as described by Mintzberg58
. All three alternatives are very laborious and not easy
to be implemented. We tried doing so in some tests, but did not succeed. They also resulted in a lot of discussion
during the designing of the MIG model. The practitioners could not reach a consensus and suggested finding out in
practice a framework that delivered the best results.20
Finally we found an easy and simple solution without the complexity of adding another framework. We used the
nine focus areas of the maturity part of the MIG model. By adding two statements for each of the nine focus areas of
hard and soft governance, we expanded the questionnaire to deliver information for the ‘informal organization’. The
questionnaire includes formal and informal statements for each focus area. For example: ‘Decision-making on IT
investments and projects is formally organized’. Furthermore, we added two control statements to check the
consistency in the answers of the participant; which in total makes 20 statements.
By using the same focus areas as in the maturity model, we do not add complexity and expect to collect useful
information on the context of each focus area in the FAMM-part of the MIG model.
We did not add a model for “sector”; because researchers know to which organization and sector the data belong.

Advanced organizations ensure that standards are regularly

In the ICITS context, we distinguish four phases of a

communication and convincing users as well as stakehold-

staff as well as the initiation of subsequent ICITS that can

5. Discussion
The integration of results from the 46 studies included in the evi­
dence base confirms the cumulative and distinct role of the alignment
between financial governanceand IT governance and provides empirical
evidence supporting the synergistic governance approach. In their
broader setting, the evidence confirms the continued significant and
positive role in financial performance played by the classical structures
related to financial governance, such as board composition, audit and
control committees, governance indices, ownership structure, and
quality of disclosure, in line with what has been reported in the corpo­
rate governance literature in general (Benvenuto et al., 2021; Garad
et al., 2021). Nevertheless, the present review also confirms that all
those structures are progressively also relying on the role provided by
the digital infrastructure and the related IT-control systems.
The patterns reported in Tables 4 and 5 show that positive outcomes
are consistently associated with combinations of clusters for instance,
structural board mechanisms together with risk and compliance
frameworks and IT-based information integrity rather than with any
single governance mechanism in isolation. The first cross-study pattern
reveals that the factors of board structure (BS), board independence
(IND), and the quality of governance measures (GQ, CGdisc, ICG) sys­
tematically and positively relate to ROA, ROE, and Tobin's Q in
Malaysia, Vietnam, Romania, Italy, and the MENA countries. These
findings are consistent with the frameworks proposed by the agency and
resource dependence theory, where the primary factors in reducing in­
formation asymmetry and improving decision-making quality are
monitoring intensity and the application of different forms and levels of
expertise. However, evidence from technology-intensive settings con­
firms that the effectiveness of the first-mentioned factors, set forth in the
frameworks, can be optimized when combined with the use of IT
governance in a way that aims to guarantee the quality and timeliness of
the digital information available for financial systems. In other words,
financial governance relies on IT governance.
The other pattern revolves around ownership structures. The
convergence on the negative impact on family ownership (FAMOWN-),
foreign ownership (FO-), and managerial ownership (MGO-) across
Indonesia, Pakistan, and Bangladesh provides evidence that a lack in
monitoring structures and transparency results from concentrated
ownership structures. The role of this review lies in the observation that
these flaws can now be exacerbated in the digital space, where the
alignment on financial controls and oversight, monitoring, and IT in
firms with concentrated ownership structures yields performance vari­
ability. The institutional ownership structure (INSTOWN+) and
governance-efficiency factors (GEFF+) always have uniformly positive
affects because they instill disciplined monitoring structures in the
framework, ensuring the institutionalization process of IT-governance.
The most prominent evidence on synergistic governance has been
observed in studies where IT governance has been explicitly combined
with financial and corporate governance models. Al Romaihi et al., in
2023 confirmed the positive impact on ROA and ROE ratios, where
corporate governance controls become stronger with the effect brought
by the role of IT knowledge on the company board. Vejseli et al., in 2022
argued that both general and agile models bring performance
improvement through alignment, and their work supported the model
focusing on alignment ability. Similarly, Ilmudeen in 2022 has also
added evidence in favor of synergistic governance, where IT-enabled
dynamic capabilities have played an important role in improving per­
formance and agility.
Across the 46 studies, these clusters do not appear as isolated ele­
ments but as configurations that co-occur in practice. For example,
several banking and corporate-governance studies report that indepen­
dent boards, active audit committees, and ownership structures (struc­
tural oversight) are associated with better financial outcomes only when
combined with robust internal-control and risk-management frame­
works (risk & compliance) that are supported by reliable, IT-enabled
reporting and disclosure (information integrity). In higher education
and service organisations, improved institutional performance and
innovation are observed where IT and business strategies are aligned
(alignment & strategic integration) and where organisations have
developed IT-enabled agility and innovation capabilities (dynamic ca­
pabilities) on top of basic financial and information controls. These
cross-study patterns underpin the grouping of mechanisms into the five
SGMM clusters and the claim that the clusters work synergistically
rather than independently.

readiness_statement: Platform-process tension (the platform must be versatile enough for complex organizational processes yet promote scalable standard functionality); platform-people tension (citizen-developer autonomy vs. technical safeguards); and process-people tension (domain-expert autonomy to improve their own workflows vs. cross-unit consistency, compliance, and interoperability) are three empirically distinguishable tension types, each requiring its own paired flexibility/standardisation guideline rather than a single governance lever.
mechanism: Cross-case thematic analysis of 57 interviews (IT professionals, citizen developers, managers, platform experts) across SoftCo and TechCo, organized around the three canonical LCNC elements (platform, process, people) identified in prior literature.
operationalization_hint: When designing governance for decentralized/citizen-driven technology development (LCNC or analogous business-unit-led initiatives), explicitly diagnose which of the three tension types (platform-process, platform-people, process-people) is at stake for a given initiative before selecting a governance response -- a single generic "more/less control" policy will not fit all three.
rationale: The two-case, 57-interview study identifies three flexibility-standardisation tension types and derives paired guidelines for them. The CF accurately preserves the platform-process, platform-people, and process-people distinction and its implication that governance needs to diagnose the relevant tension rather than rely on one generic control setting.

these platforms, such as shadow IT and technical debt. Striking the right balance is difficult—too much flexibility can compro-
mise stability, while too much standardisation can stifle the autonomy and creativity that make LCNC platforms valuable in
the first place. This study explores flexibility–standardisation tensions in LCNC development through an investigation of two
multinational technology firms with differing LCNC maturity levels, both using ServiceNow. Drawing from 57 interviews,
we identify three types of flexibility-­ standardisation tensions shaped by three key elements of LCNC development: the plat-
form itself, the people using the platform and the organisational processes targeted for improvement. We derive six guidelines
used to navigate flexibility–standardisation tensions and demonstrate how these are applied across different stages of LCNC
maturity. Building on these insights, we provide concrete, context-­ sensitive recommendations to help organisations adapt the
guidelines to their specific environments. We conclude with forward-­ looking reflections on how firms can dynamically make

in LCNC Development
At both SoftCo and TechCo, we identified multiple types of
flexibility-­ standardisation tensions. We provide examples from
our case partners, illustrating how the opposing forces of flex-
ibility and standardisation in LCNC development contribute to
these tensions. We categorise these tensions according to the
three elements of LCNC development (platform, process and
people).
4.1   |   Platform-­ Process Tension
This tension type addresses the relationship between the plat-
form's functionalities and the organisation's processes and
workflows that may be improved through LCNC development.
The platform must offer enough versatility to address diverse
and complex organisational processes, but must simultaneously
promote efficiencies (i.e., standard functionalities) that can be
scaled. A SoftCo product owner emphasised this ‘mismatch’ be-
tween the platform's capabilities and the company's processes:
‘We sometimes write a lot of code on the Now Platform because
of our complex customer requirements. As we're a large orga-
nization with intricate business processes, low-­ code solutions
alone sometimes cannot fulfil our requirements’. A TechCo
training and change manager also summarised this platform-­
process tension: ‘The platform is quite extensive and offers
many built-­ in functionalities that we could use out of the box.
The downside, however, is that we often run up against the plat-
form's limitations, where further improvement isn't possible’.
4.2   |   People-­ Platform Tension
This type of tension revolves around balancing user autonomy
to build applications or improve workflows while ensuring there
are technical safeguards in place. On the one hand, a great deal
of the value of LCNC development lies in the empowerment as-
pect of citizen developers, as one citizen developer at TechCo ex-
plained: ‘Now I feel like I'm part of the magic—I can do a lot on
myownwithoutneedingmuchscriptingknowledge.InEasyHR,
I'm now able to do things that are quite similar to what my col-
leagues in IT can do. It really feels like we're on the same level
and can collaborate as equals’. However, a lack of guardrails for
citizen developers can lead to issues such as poorly designed ap-
plications, data breaches, or other inefficiencies. A SoftCo devel-
oper noted: ‘If people with little or no programming experience
start developing applications and have unrestricted access to
company data—without fully understanding what they're doing
or how the tools work—it can quickly become a serious problem.
For example, sensitive data might be unintentionally exposed ex-
ternally, which is obviously something you want to avoid’.
4.3   |   Process-­ People Tension
While this tension type is highly relevant to LCNC development,
it also extends beyond LCNC development to the broader organ-
isational domain, as it deals with the balancing act of providing
autonomy to employees to customise and improve organisational
workflows without excessive oversight. On the one hand, as do-
main experts often know their workflows best, allowing them
flexibility can provide both operational efficiencies and a sense
of empowerment. One of TechCo's project managers noted: ‘We
don't need programmers with deep coding expertise. What we
needareprocessexpertswhounderstandthesystemwellenough
to configure it effectively and ensure it serves its intended pur-
pose. It's a fundamentally different approach from what we had
in the past’. Nevertheless, this must be balanced with the need
for standardised procedures that ensure consistency, compliance
and interoperability across teams and departments, as a TechCo
product owner highlighted: ‘The exchange between the Epics6

paper_authors: Viljoen, A.; Stelzl, B.; Yang, M.; Nguyen, J.; Hein, A.; Elshan, E.; Krcmar, H.
authors: Viljoen, A.; Stelzl, B.; Yang, M.; Nguyen, J.; Hein, A.; Elshan, E.; Krcmar, H.
raw_condition_label: LCNC (and by extension, decentralized-development) governance must be treated as a dynamic capability that evolves with organizational maturity rather than a static framework -- flexibility and standardisation are mutually reinforcing (not a fixed trade-off), and what counts as "custom" versus "standard" shifts over time as the platform and organization mature
readiness_statement: Early-maturity organizations benefit most from adhering closely to platform standards ("quick wins," foundational competency-building), while advanced-maturity organizations can productively shift toward proactive vendor co-design and greater customization; moreover, pursuing flexibility (e.g. adopting LCNC to move fast) itself often exposes and forces the harmonization of previously fragmented/outdated processes, meaning standardisation and flexibility reinforce rather than oppose each other over time -- treating either pole as a fixed, permanent policy choice is a governance failure mode.
mechanism: Cross-case comparison of SoftCo (advanced maturity, design-partnership stage) versus TechCo (earlier stage, standard-feature-reliant) plus the authors' concluding theoretical reflection explicitly reframing the flexibility-standardisation "paradox" as a dynamic, evolving "both-and" relationship rather than a static trade-off.
operationalization_hint: When evaluating or designing governance for decentralized/citizen-led technology initiatives, revisit and update the flexibility/standardisation balance periodically as organizational and platform maturity increases, rather than fixing a governance policy at initial rollout and treating deviations from it as permanent violations to be suppressed.
rationale: The authors explicitly frame LCNC governance as a dynamic capability that evolves with organizational change and maturity, rather than a fixed one-off framework.

paper_authors: Mentzingen Moraes, A.J.; Rocha, Á.
authors: Mentzingen Moraes, A.J.; Rocha, Á.
raw_condition_label: a 12-area x 3-sub-indicator (work-result, delivery-commitment, customer-satisfaction) monitoring panel, derived by synthesizing 26 established IT maturity models into a non-redundant set of areas grouped into planning/execution/control phases, gives a lightweight, continuous alternative to periodic full maturity-model assessments for tracking ITG alignment with strategic planning
readiness_statement: Rather than periodically re-running a full maturity assessment (COBIT, CMMI, etc.), an organization can track a compact panel of 36 sub-indicators (3 per each of 12 IT areas: percentage of work completed; percentage completed on schedule/budget; percentage completed, on schedule/budget, AND formally accepted by the customer) calculated via a standardized percentage formula against organization-set maximum/minimum goals, enabling continuous, low-overhead monitoring between full maturity assessments.
mechanism: Design Science Research methodology (Wieringa's process): problem investigation (bibliographic gap analysis across 9 databases), solution design (synthesis of 26 maturity models into 12 non-redundant IT monitoring areas), and validation via three simulation rounds within one real organization, culminating in reusable spreadsheet and guideline artefacts.
operationalization_hint: For organizations needing continuous, lightweight visibility into ITG execution between full periodic maturity assessments, consider adopting a compact indicator panel (work-completion rate, on-schedule/on-budget delivery rate, and formally-accepted-delivery rate) per governance-relevant IT area, rather than relying solely on infrequent, resource-intensive full maturity-model audits.
rationale: PI2M-ITGov explicitly defines 12 monitoring areas, one KMI and three work-result/delivery/customer-satisfaction sub-KMIs per area. It is a proposed measurement artifact.

raw_condition_label: a fixed, unweighted indicator panel risks misrepresenting what constitutes good IT governance for a specific organizational context -- sector-appropriate weighting (e.g. security-heavy for finance, knowledge-management-heavy for media, project-management-heavy for manufacturing) is needed, and real-world piloting reveals indicator-scoring failure modes (unavailable data, contextually-confounded scores) that require human interpretation rather than purely mechanical scoring
readiness_statement: The authors note that different sectors should weight the 12 IT monitoring areas differently (e.g. a financial-sector company should weight security KMIs more heavily, a media company should weight knowledge-management KMIs more heavily); moreover, the real-world pilot at the Brazilian Government Agency documented concrete scoring anomalies requiring human interpretation -- a security-area KMI could not be evaluated because the security team was mid-review of its internal processes, and a customer-satisfaction sub-indicator showed an anomalously low score explained by unrelated staff-leave patterns rather than true service failure.
mechanism: Documented findings from the three-round implementation-assessment case study at a single Brazilian Government Agency undergoing organizational restructuring, including explicit reviewer comments recorded in the validation spreadsheet explaining anomalous scores.
operationalization_hint: When deploying a standardized IT-governance indicator panel across sectors or organizational contexts, apply sector-appropriate significance weighting rather than a uniform scheme, and build in a human-review step to catch and explain data-availability gaps or context-confounded scores (e.g. a bad score driven by unrelated organizational events) before treating raw indicator output as an accurate governance signal.
rationale: The source explicitly recommends context-specific indicator weights and documents unavailable and confounded scores requiring interpretation during the pilot. This is a bounded case-based warning against mechanical scoring.

readiness_statement: Risk appetite is modeled as an association from the Risk_Appetite class to specific Strategic_Objective instances, allowing an organization to hold near-zero risk tolerance for one objective (e.g. patient safety) while accepting much higher risk for another (e.g. pursuing innovation/reputational opportunities) within the same governance model.

raw_condition_label: emerging technology/digital-context elements should be explicitly modeled as first-class contributors that can help (mitigate) or hurt (aggravate) existing strategic risks, making visible how adopting new technology changes an organization's risk profile and not only its capability profile
readiness_statement: Digital context (e.g. cloud computing, IoT, big data, blockchain, AI) is modeled with explicit "help"/"hurt" contribution links to both hazard and opportunity risks at the strategic level -- e.g. cloud adoption can aggravate data-loss risk (hurt) while simultaneously improving real-time information sharing (help) -- rather than being assessed only for its alignment/value contribution to strategic objectives.
mechanism: Meta-model extension illustrated via the Saint-Romain cloud-adoption example, where the same digital-context element (cloud computing) is shown simultaneously helping one risk/opportunity pair and hurting another.
operationalization_hint: When assessing the adoption of a new technology at the governance level, explicitly trace both its value-alignment contribution AND its help/hurt effect on existing strategic risks -- a purely capability- or alignment-focused technology assessment (as in most BITA models) will miss the risk-profile changes that same technology introduces.
page_or_section: Section 5.2 (Model-based Representation of Risk), Fig. 2, pp. 540-661
rationale: The strategic risk meta-model explicitly represents digital-context elements with help/hurt links, illustrated by a technology-adoption example. It is a model-based representation contribution.

paper_title: Information Technology Governance Awareness: A Proposed Formula for Assessment
title: Information Technology Governance Awareness: A Proposed Formula for Assessment
paper_authors: Uky, Y.; Harmadji, D.E.
authors: Uky, Y.; Harmadji, D.E.
raw_condition_label: existing IT governance maturity assessment methods (based on COBIT best practices) focus only on objects/artifacts (processes, controls) and do not focus on subjects/stakeholders (their awareness, buy-in, understanding) -- a persistent measurement gap that may cause maturity assessments to miss a critical predictor of implementation success
readiness_statement: The authors identify that the standard approach to determining ITG implementation success (COBIT-based maturity-level calculation) evaluates only the artifacts/objects of governance, while the parties involved (stakeholders) have "a very significant influence in determining the success rate of implementing IT Governance practices, especially in awareness" -- a gap this paper's awareness formula was specifically designed to address, motivated by prior research showing a positive correlation between awareness and governance implementation success.
mechanism: Motivating problem statement grounded in a literature review of prior ITG-awareness research (including a Malaysian senior-manager study establishing the awareness-implementation correlation) and the authors' own prior published work on ITG critical success factors and barriers.
operationalization_hint: When evaluating why an organization's IT governance implementation stalled despite passing artifact/process-based maturity checks (COBIT, ITIL, etc.), check whether stakeholder awareness (knowledge, attitude, and enacted behavior toward governance rules) was ever assessed -- a governance program can look mature on paper (controls, processes documented) while lacking the subject-side awareness needed to sustain it.
rationale: The paper identifies the object-versus-subject measurement gap and motivates a stakeholder awareness assessment that covers knowledge, attitude, and behavior. It is a problem-framing and measurement proposition, not causal validation.

readiness_statement: Because organizational structure alone cannot enforce every desired IT-related behavior (e.g. an autonomous business-unit structure can still be paired with enterprise-wide IT architecture principles or centrally-vetted investment approval to achieve enterprise cost/synergy objectives without reorganizing), firms can achieve conflicting synergy and autonomy objectives simultaneously by using IT governance mechanisms to fill the specific gaps left by organizational structure, rather than repeatedly restructuring.

We propose that IT governance design should encompass the following four steps. 
First, identify the firm’s needs for synergy and autonomy.  Senior managers are often enamored 
of the potential to derive business value from synergistic efforts like cross-selling, standard 
technology platforms or enterpri se-wide business processes. We encourage management teams 
to consider realistically both th e benefits and costs of synergies. Synergy-autonomy tradeoffs 
force senior managers to make tough decisions  and communicate those decisions throughout the 
enterprise. Clarifying those decisi ons establishes the parameters for the design of IT governance 
and accompanying managerial incentives.  
Second, establish the role of organization structure.  Firms have long relied on organization 
structure to create the context for achieving organizational objectives. For some time, this 
resulted in pendulum-like swings between central ized and decentralized organizational forms. 
Over time, firms pursued both centralization and decentralization simultaneously by introducing 
more matrixed reporting relationships. The complexity of matrices can overwhelm managers and 
limit effectiveness. By establishing organizational priorities for autonomy and synergy, firms can 
introduce organizational designs and incentive  systems to accomplish their priorities.

raw_condition_label: an EA organization's placement in the corporate structure (embedded within IT, staff to the CIO, a corporate-level division on par with IT/business, or a corporate staff department reporting to the CEO) determines a monotonic tradeoff between ease of setup and authority over business (not just IT) architecture -- only CEO-level placement enables genuine corporate governance authority, but at the cost of requiring company-wide behavioral and incentive changes
readiness_statement: Four typical EA-organization placements were compared: (1) EA embedded as one team within IT -- simplest to set up, but structurally disconnected from business departments, limited to an IT-centric view of business capabilities, and easily becomes a bottleneck with no authority to compel business-side data or collaboration; (2) EA as a staff department to the CIO -- shifts EA toward strategic IT activities and allows delegating data-collection to IT teams, but remains business-disconnected; (3) EA as a corporate-level division on par with IT and business departments -- improves business relevance and collaboration but has only advisory (not enforcement) power over peer departments; (4) EA as a corporate staff department reporting directly to the CEO -- enables a genuine corporate governance approach with enforcement authority across all departments, but requires enabling/training people company-wide and setting proper incentives, representing the largest organizational change.
mechanism: Comparative framework synthesized from the lead author's first-hand professional experience in EA organizations of types (1)-(3) at a major logistics company, cross-referenced against practitioner literature and the general EAM literature on organizational placement.
operationalization_hint: When advising on where to place a newly-formed (or restructuring) EA function, do not treat organizational placement as a minor implementation detail -- map the intended placement against this four-level hierarchy first, since the authority to compel business-side collaboration and enforce architecture standards (not just produce artifacts) scales directly with how close EA sits to the CEO, and each step up this hierarchy requires a correspondingly larger change-management and incentive-design investment.
rationale: The masterclass compares four EA-placement options and their authority/change tradeoffs, drawing materially on professional experience. It is retained as a practitioner-framework proposition rather than general causal evidence.

They are basically aiming at developing a more flexible method with respect to
EA, that does not only adapt a framework, but implements a methodologybased on
business needs. Such a methodology is not strictly aiming at long term objectives
only, but that can be adjusted to changes in objectives easily. Such a methodology
should not only print or create a lot of documents, but focus on those documents
that are really needed by other departments. This should foster the provision of
information and visualisation as needed by stakeholders.
The EA organisation should not start with collecting as much data as possible
and then create fancy posters, but understand business needs first. It should then
specifically get this kind of information, so that it can provide immediate benefit
by delivering relevant (i.e. helpful) visualisation. This will require a clear value
proposition based on business needs. The following sections provide an overview
on some ideas how such an organisation could look like.
